citation: Frege, G. (1892). Über Sinn und Bedeutung. *Zeitschrift für Philosophie und philosophische Kritik*, N.F. 100(1), 25–50. (English: "On Sense and Reference" / "On Sense and Nominatum"; anthologized e.g. in Martinich (ed.), *The Philosophy of Language*, OUP.)
why: Frege asks why "the Morning Star is the Evening Star" is informative while "the Morning Star is the Morning Star" is not. His answer is that an expression has a *reference* (the object it picks out) and a *sense* (its mode of presentation). The distinction underlies all later semantics, and it is the original version of the question "same referent, different representation", which now comes up for embeddings and framing.
focus: whole (short); the identity puzzle at the opening, the telescope analogy, and the treatment of sentences (reference = truth-value) and of indirect speech.
access: free: https://www.deutschestextarchiv.de/book/show/frege_sinn_1892 (German original, Deutsches Textarchiv, CC BY-NC; plain text at https://www.deutschestextarchiv.de/book/download_txt/frege_sinn_1892)
translation: 土屋俊訳「意義と意味について」, 黒田亘・野本和幸編『哲学論集』(フレーゲ著作集), 勁草書房, 1999.
verified: https://clarin.bbaw.de/en/objects/dta:298/ ; https://www.deutschestextarchiv.de/book/show/frege_sinn_1892 ; translation: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/ゴットロープ・フレーゲ

citation: Russell, B. (1905). On Denoting. *Mind*, 14(4) [whole no. 56], 479–493. doi:10.1093/mind/XIV.4.479
why: Russell shows how "The present King of France is bald" can be meaningful even though nothing answers to the description. He paraphrases it into quantified logical form: there is exactly one King of France, and he is bald. This became the model of "analysis": a sentence's grammatical form can mislead you about its logical form.
focus: whole; the three puzzles (identity, excluded middle with "the King of France", negative existentials) and their solution.

citation: Wittgenstein, L. (1922). *Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus* (trans. C. K. Ogden with F. P. Ramsey; intro. B. Russell). London: Kegan Paul. First published in German as "Logisch-philosophische Abhandlung", *Annalen der Naturphilosophie*, 1921.
why: The *Tractatus* holds that a meaningful proposition is a logical picture of a possible state of affairs, and that whatever cannot be pictured (ethics, logic's own form) can only be "shown". It inspired the Vienna Circle and is the foil for Wittgenstein's own later work. Read it to see the strongest version of the idea that language mirrors the world's structure.
focus: the seven main numbered propositions and their first-level comments, then follow the numbering down only where needed. Read with Soames Vol. 1 Part Three.
access: free: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/5740 (Ogden translation, public domain in the US)
translation: 野矢茂樹訳『論理哲学論考』岩波文庫, 2003.
verified: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/5740 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tractatus_Logico-Philosophicus ; translation: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/論理哲学論考

citation: Wittgenstein, L. (1953/2009). *Philosophical Investigations* (trans. G. E. M. Anscombe, P. M. S. Hacker & J. Schulte; rev. 4th ed., ed. Hacker & Schulte). Chichester: Wiley-Blackwell. (German–English facing text.)
why: The later Wittgenstein rejects his own picture theory. For a large class of cases the meaning of a word is its use in a "language-game", a rule-governed social activity. Concepts like "game" hang together by family resemblance rather than shared essences, and following a rule is a public practice, not a private mental act. This is the philosophical ancestor of usage-based and distributional views of meaning.
focus: §1 (Augustine's picture of language), §23 (multiplicity of language-games), §§66–71 (family resemblance), §§138–242 (rule-following, esp. §201), §243 ff. (private language).
translation: 鬼界彰夫訳『哲学探究』講談社, 2020. (Older: 藤本隆志訳, ウィトゲンシュタイン全集8, 大修館書店, 1976.)

citation: Quine, W. V. O. (1951). Main Trends in Recent Philosophy: Two Dogmas of Empiricism. *The Philosophical Review*, 60(1), 20–43. doi:10.2307/2181906. Reprinted in Quine, *From a Logical Point of View* (Harvard UP, 1953).
why: Quine attacks two dogmas: the line between truths true "by meaning" (analytic) and truths true "by fact" (synthetic), and the idea that each statement can be tested against experience on its own. His alternative is a "web of belief" in which experience confronts our theories only as a whole, and any statement can be kept if we adjust enough elsewhere. It is one of the most influential papers in twentieth-century analytic philosophy.
focus: whole (about 24 pages); the closing section on empiricism without the dogmas states the "web of belief" picture.
translation: 飯田隆訳『論理的観点から――論理と哲学をめぐる九章』勁草書房, 1992 (contains 「経験主義の二つのドグマ」).
verified: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2307/2181906 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_Dogmas_of_Empiricism ; translation: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/ウィラード・ヴァン・オーマン・クワイン

citation: Quine, W. V. O. (1960). *Word and Object*. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. New edition 2013, foreword by Patricia S. Churchland, preface by Dagfinn Føllesdal (ISBN 9780262518314).
why: Quine imagines a linguist translating a completely unknown language from behavioural evidence alone. He argues that incompatible translation manuals can fit all the evidence equally well, so there is no fact of the matter about what "gavagai" refers to: rabbit, rabbit-stage or undetached rabbit-part. This "indeterminacy of translation" is the deepest philosophical treatment of the question of what fixes meaning given only input-output behaviour.
focus: Ch. 2 (meaning and translation: radical translation, stimulus meaning, "gavagai"); Ch. 1 for the setting.
translation: 大出晁・宮館恵訳『ことばと対象』勁草書房, 1984.
verified: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_and_Object ; https://penguinrandomhouse.ca/books/656758/word-and-object-new-edition-by-willard-van-orman-quine-foreword-by-patricia-smith-churchland-preface-to-the-new-edition-by-dagfinn-fllesdal/9780262518314 ; translation: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/ウィラード・ヴァン・オーマン・クワイン

citation: Austin, J. L. (1962). *How to Do Things with Words* (The William James Lectures delivered at Harvard University in 1955; ed. J. O. Urmson). Oxford: Clarendon Press. 2nd ed. 1975, ed. J. O. Urmson & M. Sbisà (Clarendon / Harvard UP).
why: Austin notices that many utterances do not describe anything; they *do* something, such as promising, naming a ship, or saying "I do". He separates the act of saying something (locution), what you do in saying it (illocution: warning, ordering), and its effects (perlocution: alarming, persuading). Speech-act theory is the philosophical basis for treating communication as action, which matters directly for crisis and risk communication.
focus: whole (short lectures); performatives and felicity conditions in the early lectures; the locutionary/illocutionary/perlocutionary distinction and the closing taxonomy of illocutionary forces.
translation: 飯野勝己訳『言語と行為――いかにして言葉でものごとを行うか』講談社学術文庫, 2019 (earlier: 坂本百大訳『言語と行為』大修館書店, 1978).
verified: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/How_to_Do_Things_with_Words ; translation: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/ジョン・L・オースティン

citation: Grice, H. P. (1975). Logic and Conversation. In P. Cole & J. L. Morgan (eds.), *Syntax and Semantics, Vol. 3: Speech Acts* (pp. 41–58). New York: Academic Press. Reprinted in Grice, *Studies in the Way of Words* (Harvard UP, 1989), pp. 22–40.
why: Grice explains how we routinely mean more than we say. Hearers assume speakers are cooperative, meaning informative, truthful, relevant and clear (the maxims of Quantity, Quality, Relation and Manner). When a speaker seems to flout a maxim, the hearer infers a "conversational implicature". This is the foundation of pragmatics, of Rational Speech Act models, and of analyses of misleading-but-true communication.
focus: whole. Read with its companion, Grice, H. P. (1957), "Meaning", *The Philosophical Review* 66(3), 377–388 (doi:10.2307/2182440), which defines speaker meaning as an intention to produce an effect in a hearer through the hearer's recognition of that intention.
translation: 清塚邦彦訳『論理と会話』勁草書房, 1998 (partial translation of *Studies in the Way of Words*).
verified: https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/implicature/ (bibliography: "Cole & Morgan 1975: 41–58. Reprinted in Grice 1989: 22–40") ; companion: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2307/2182440 ; translation: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/ポール・グライス

citation: Kripke, S. A. (1980). *Naming and Necessity*. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press. (Lectures given at Princeton, January 1970; first printed in D. Davidson & G. Harman (eds.), *Semantics of Natural Language*, Reidel, 1972.)
why: Kripke argues that proper names are not disguised descriptions. A name is a "rigid designator" that picks out the same individual in every possible world, and it gets its reference from a causal-historical chain of use, not from a description in the speaker's head. He also argues that some necessary truths, like "water is H2O", are discovered empirically. Together these overturned the Frege–Russell orthodoxy.
focus: Lecture I (critique of descriptivism; rigidity), Lecture II (the Gödel/Schmidt case; the causal picture), Lecture III (natural kinds; necessary a posteriori). The 1980 preface is a useful summary.
translation: 八木沢敬・野家啓一訳『名指しと必然性――様相の形而上学と心身問題』産業図書, 1985.
verified: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_and_Necessity ; https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0674598466 ; translation: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/名指しと必然性

citation: Putnam, H. (1975). The Meaning of "Meaning". In K. Gunderson (ed.), *Language, Mind, and Knowledge*, Minnesota Studies in the Philosophy of Science, Vol. 7 (pp. 131–193). Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press.
why: Putnam's Twin Earth thought experiment shows that two people in identical mental states can mean different things by "water" if their environments differ (H2O vs. XYZ). Hence "meanings just ain't in the head". He adds the "division of linguistic labour": ordinary speakers defer to experts to fix what "elm" or "gold" refers to. This is semantic externalism, and it bears on whether a text-only model can mean anything.
focus: whole; the Twin Earth sections, the elm/beech example, the "division of linguistic labor" (and its universality hypothesis), and the later sections on stereotypes and semantic markers.
access: free: https://conservancy.umn.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/09012d92-398e-40b0-9f60-a3f37f05d2a5/content (direct PDF, University of Minnesota Digital Conservancy)

citation: Lewis, D. (1969). *Convention: A Philosophical Study*. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press. Reissued Oxford: Blackwell, 2002 (foreword by W. V. Quine).
why: Lewis uses Schelling-style game theory to define a convention: a regularity that solves a recurring coordination problem and that persists because everyone expects everyone else to conform, under common knowledge. He then uses this to explain the "platitude that language is ruled by convention", treating meaning as an equilibrium of signalling. This is the main hinge between analytic philosophy and game theory, and the ancestor of signalling-game models of the evolution of meaning.
focus: Ch. I (coordination and convention; salience), and the last two chapters, "Signalling Systems" and "Conventions of Language". Free companion: Lewis, D. (1975), "Languages and Language", in Gunderson (ed.), Minnesota Studies Vol. 7, pp. 3–35, PDF at https://conservancy.umn.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/361dde7c-8e3e-463c-a74b-eb5d79ce7f8a/content (handle https://hdl.handle.net/11299/185227).

citation: Gettier, E. L. (1963). Is Justified True Belief Knowledge? *Analysis*, 23(6), 121–123. doi:10.1093/analys/23.6.121
why: In under three pages, Gettier gives two cases in which someone has a justified, true belief that is true only by luck, so intuitively it is not knowledge. This broke the classical "justified true belief" analysis and launched sixty years of work on epistemic luck, reliability and safety. It is the field's standard example of a counterexample defeating a definition.
focus: whole (Case I: Smith, Jones and the ten coins; Case II: the Ford/Barcelona disjunction).

citation: Goldman, A. I. (1999). *Knowledge in a Social World*. Oxford: Clarendon Press / New York: Oxford University Press. 407 pp.
why: Goldman founded "veritistic" social epistemology: social practices such as testimony, argument, media, law and science are judged by how well they raise a community's level of true belief. The book treats the "marketplace of ideas" and communication technologies as empirical epistemic questions. That makes it the most direct philosophical foundation for misinformation research.
focus: Part I chs. 1–3 (postmodern resistance; truth; the framework), Part II chs. 4–7 (testimony; argumentation; technology and economics of communication; speech regulation and the marketplace of ideas), ch. 8 (science).

citation: Coady, C. A. J. (1992). *Testimony: A Philosophical Study*. Oxford: Clarendon Press.
why: Most of what we know comes from other people's say-so, yet classical epistemology treated testimony as second-rate. Coady argues against "reductionism", the Humean idea that we must check a source's reliability from our own observation before trusting it. He holds that testimony is a basic source of evidence, like perception. This sets the terms of the reductionism vs. anti-reductionism debate on trust in sources.
focus: Part 1 "The Problematic", Part 2 "The Tradition" (the reductive and analogical approaches; Reid's "Scottish fundamentalism"), Part 3 "The Solution"; Part 5 "The Applications" (experts, history, law) as relevant.

citation: Hempel, C. G., & Oppenheim, P. (1948). Studies in the Logic of Explanation. *Philosophy of Science*, 15(2), 135–175. doi:10.1086/286983
why: This paper states the deductive-nomological ("covering law") model: to explain an event is to deduce it from general laws plus initial conditions, so explanation and prediction have the same logical form. It is the benchmark that every later theory of explanation (causal, unificationist, mechanistic) defines itself against, and it frames the "explanation vs. prediction" debate in computational social science.
focus: the opening sections that state the basic D-N pattern and its conditions of adequacy. Companion on confirmation and the raven paradox: Hempel, C. G. (1945), "Studies in the Logic of Confirmation (I.)", *Mind* 54(213), 1–26, doi:10.1093/mind/LIV.213.1. Hempel's essays are collected in *Aspects of Scientific Explanation and Other Essays in the Philosophy of Science* (Free Press, 1965, 504 pp.).

citation: Popper, K. R. (1959). *The Logic of Scientific Discovery*. London: Hutchinson. (Trans. of *Logik der Forschung*, Springer, 1934 [imprint 1935].) Routledge Classics ed., 2002, 544 pp.
why: Popper argues that no number of confirming observations can verify a universal theory, but a single reproducible counter-instance can refute it. So what makes a theory scientific is falsifiability, and good theories are bold ones that forbid a lot and survive severe tests ("corroboration"). It is the root of the demarcation problem and of the falsificationist logic built into significance testing.
focus: Part I chs. 1 "A Survey of Some Fundamental Problems" and 2; Part II ch. 4 "Falsifiability", ch. 5 "The Problem of the Empirical Basis", ch. 6 "Degrees of Testability", ch. 10 "Corroboration, or How a Theory Stands up to Tests".
translation: 大内義一・森博訳『科学的発見の論理』(上・下) 恒星社厚生閣, 1971–72.
verified: https://www.routledge.com/The-Lic/Popper/p/book/9780415278447 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Logic_of_Scientific_Discovery ; translation: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/科学的発見の論理

citation: Kuhn, T. S. (1962/2012). *The Structure of Scientific Revolutions* (4th ed., 50th anniversary edition, with an introductory essay by Ian Hacking). Chicago: University of Chicago Press. 264 pp.
why: Kuhn's history shows that science mostly runs as "normal science", puzzle-solving within a shared paradigm. Anomalies pile up into crisis, and crises are resolved by revolutions after which old and new paradigms are partly "incommensurable". The book made the social organisation of science a philosophical topic, and it is the source of "paradigm shift" and much of science-of-science and community-dynamics thinking.
focus: Hacking's introductory essay; chs. II–V (normal science, puzzle-solving, priority of paradigms); chs. VI–X (anomaly, crisis, revolutions as changes of world view); Postscript–1969 (the "disciplinary matrix" and community structure).
translation: 青木薫訳『科学革命の構造 新版』みすず書房, 2023 (from the 4th ed., with Hacking's essay); earlier 中山茂訳, みすず書房, 1971.

citation: Lakatos, I. (1970). Falsification and the Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes. In I. Lakatos & A. Musgrave (eds.), *Criticism and the Growth of Knowledge* (pp. 91–196). Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/CBO9781139171434.009
why: Lakatos sits between Popper and Kuhn. The unit of appraisal is not a single theory but a research programme: a protected "hard core" surrounded by a "protective belt" of auxiliary hypotheses. A programme is progressive if its modifications predict novel facts, and degenerating if they only patch failures after the fact. This gives a practical vocabulary for judging whether a research line, including your own, is still productive.
focus: the sections contrasting dogmatic, naive and sophisticated falsificationism, and the section on the methodology of research programmes (negative and positive heuristic).
translation: 森博監訳『批判と知識の成長』木鐸社, 1985 (translation of the whole volume).
verified: https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/criticism-and-the-growth-of-knowledge/falsification-and-the-methodology-of-scientific-research-programmes/B1AAD974814D6E7BF35E6449691AA58F ; translation: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/ラカトシュ・イムレ

citation: van Fraassen, B. C. (1980). *The Scientific Image*. Oxford: Clarendon Press. 235 pp.
why: Van Fraassen defends "constructive empiricism": science aims only at theories that are *empirically adequate*, meaning true about what is observable. Accepting a theory need not mean believing its claims about unobservables. It is the strongest modern anti-realist position and the standard opponent in the realism debate, and it applies directly to how we should read latent constructs in models.
focus: whole; read alongside Godfrey-Smith ch. 12 (§12.6 "Van Fraassen's View").
translation: 丹治信春訳『科学的世界像』紀伊國屋書店, 1986.
verified: https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0198244274 ; translation: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/バス・ファン・フラーセン

citation: Howson, C., & Urbach, P. (2005). *Scientific Reasoning: The Bayesian Approach* (3rd ed.). Chicago/La Salle, IL: Open Court. 327 pp. ISBN 978-0-8126-9578-6. (1st ed. 1989; 2nd ed. 1993; the 3rd ed. is often cited as 2006.)
why: This is the standard philosophical defence of Bayesian confirmation theory. Evidence confirms a hypothesis when it raises its probability, and the same machinery is used to resolve the raven paradox, the Duhem problem and ad hoc hypotheses. It also mounts a sustained critique of Fisherian and Neyman–Pearson significance testing, so it doubles as a philosophy-of-statistics text for a working quantitative researcher.
focus: Ch. 1 (problem of induction; Popper); Ch. 3 "The Laws of Probability" (Dutch book, updating rules); Ch. 4 "Bayesian Induction: Deterministic Theories" (4.d The Ravens Paradox, 4.e The Duhem Problem, 4.g Ad Hoc Hypotheses); Ch. 5 "Classical Inference: Significance Tests and Estimation".

citation: Magnus, P. D., Button, T., Trueman, R., & Zach, R. (with J. R. Loftis & A. Thomas-Bolduc) (2025). *forall x: Calgary. An Introduction to Formal Logic* (Fall 2025 ed.). Open Logic Project, CC BY 4.0.
why: This is a free, rigorous, widely adopted first course in formal logic: validity, truth-functional logic, truth tables, first-order logic with identity, and natural deduction. Analytic philosophy assumes you can see the logical form under a sentence. This is the fastest legal way to get that skill, and its "use and mention" chapter is a hidden gem for anyone who writes about language models.
focus: Part I "Key notions of logic" (chs. 1–3); Part II "Truth-functional logic" (chs. 4–8, incl. ch. 8 "Use and mention"); Part III "Truth tables" (chs. 9–15); then the first-order logic parts as needed.
verified: https://forallx.openlogicproject.org/ (front matter and contents read from the PDF)

citation: Beaney, M., & Raysmith, T. (2003; substantive revision 2024). Analysis. *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*.
why: "Analysis" is the method that gives analytic philosophy its name, and this entry explains what it has meant: decomposition, Russell-style logical paraphrase, Carnapian explication, Oxford linguistic analysis, and today's "conceptual engineering". It is the best short account of *how* analytic philosophers work.
focus: §1 (characterizations of analysis), §6 (conceptions of analysis in analytic philosophy) and its supplement "Conceptions of Analysis in Analytic Philosophy" (Frege, Russell, Moore, Wittgenstein, Carnap and explication, Oxford linguistic philosophy, conceptual analysis, conceptual engineering).

citation: Godfrey-Smith, P. (2003). *Theory and Reality: An Introduction to the Philosophy of Science*. Chicago: University of Chicago Press (Science and Its Conceptual Foundations). 272 pp.
why: This is the best single on-ramp to philosophy of science and the indicative text for LSE PH201. It moves from logical empiricism through Popper, Kuhn, Lakatos, Laudan and Feyerabend to the sociology of science, naturalism, the social structure of science, realism, explanation and Bayesianism. It is clear and opinionated, and it covers Feyerabend (ch. 7) and the realism debate (ch. 12), which have no standalone items here.
focus: chs. 2–7 (logical empiricism; induction and confirmation incl. §3.3 The Ravens Problem and §3.4 Goodman's new riddle; Popper; Kuhn ×2; "Lakatos, Laudan, Feyerabend, and Frameworks"); ch. 11 "Naturalism and the Social Structure of Science"; ch. 12 "Scientific Realism"; ch. 13 "Explanation"; ch. 14 "Bayesianism and Modern Theories of Evidence".

citation: Lycan, W. G. (2019). *Philosophy of Language: A Contemporary Introduction* (3rd ed.). New York/London: Routledge. 252 pp.
why: This is the standard textbook companion to the classic papers. MIT's 24.251 pairs each Lycan chapter with the original reading: Frege, Russell, Kripke, Grice, Quine, Davidson, Austin and Searle. Each chapter states a theory, gives the canonical objections, and tells you where the debate stands.
focus: ch. 1 (meaning and reference); Part I chs. 2–4 (descriptions; names: description theory vs. direct reference/causal-historical); Part II chs. 5–9 (traditional, "use", Gricean, verificationist and Davidsonian theories of meaning); Part III chs. 11–13 (pragmatics; speech acts; implicative relations).

citation: Soames, S. (2003). *Philosophical Analysis in the Twentieth Century*. Vol. 1: *The Dawn of Analysis* (411 pp.); Vol. 2: *The Age of Meaning* (479 pp.). Princeton: Princeton University Press.
why: This is a critical, argument-by-argument history of analytic philosophy from Moore and Russell through the *Tractatus*, logical positivism and Quine (Vol. 1), to ordinary-language philosophy, Davidson and Kripke (Vol. 2). Use it to see how the classic texts connect and where each argument succeeds or fails.
focus: Vol. 1 Part Two (Russell, ch. 5 "Logical Form, Grammatical Form, and the Theory of Descriptions"), Part Three (*Tractatus*, chs. 9–11), Part Four ch. 13 "The Rise and Fall of the Empiricist Criterion of Meaning", Part Five (early Quine, chs. 16–17); Vol. 2 as needed for Wittgenstein, Davidson, Kripke.

citation: Ichikawa, J. J., & Steup, M. (2001; substantive revision 2026). The Analysis of Knowledge. *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*.
why: This is the authoritative map of the post-Gettier landscape: the JTB analysis, Gettier counterexamples, no-false-lemmas, sensitivity and safety, reliabilism, epistemic luck, fake-barn cases, virtue epistemology, knowledge-first, pragmatic encroachment and contextualism.

citation: O'Connor, C., Goldberg, S., & Goldman, A. (2001; substantive revision 2024). Social Epistemology. *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*.
why: This is the closest point of contact between analytic philosophy and computational social science. It covers testimony, peer disagreement and group belief, and also formal network-epistemology models, modelling of diversity in epistemic communities, misleading online content and socio-epistemic dysfunctions such as echo chambers.
focus: §3.1 Testimony; §4 "Formal Approaches to Social Epistemology" (esp. §4.3 Network Epistemology Models, §4.4 Modeling Diversity); §5.2 Misleading Online Content; §5.3 Socio-Epistemic Dysfunctions.

citation: Lin, H. (2022). Bayesian Epistemology. *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*.
why: This entry links formal epistemology to Bayesian statistics. It opens with a tutorial (a case study, the two core norms of probabilism and conditionalization, Dutch-book foundations, the problem of priors) and then covers old evidence, uncertain learning and idealization. It is the right place to see which parts of "Bayesian" are mathematics and which are philosophical commitments.
focus: §1 "A Tutorial on Bayesian Epistemology"; §2 formalism; §4 "The Problem of the Priors"; §5.1 Old Evidence.

strand: Foundations — probability as extended logic, history, subjective probability
citation: Bayes, T. [communicated by R. Price] (1763). *An Essay towards Solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances*. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, 53, 370–418. DOI: 10.1098/rstl.1763.0053
why: This is the founding text. Bayes asks how to infer the unknown chance of an event from observed successes and failures, and answers with a "billiard table" thought experiment that amounts to a uniform prior on that chance. Price's preface frames the result as a tool for reasoning from effects back to causes. Read it for the original framing more than the mathematics.
focus: Price's covering letter and the problem statement; the billiard-table construction

strand: Foundations — probability as extended logic, history, subjective probability
citation: Laplace, P.-S. (1902). *A Philosophical Essay on Probabilities* (F. W. Truscott & F. L. Emory, Trans., from the 6th French ed.). New York: John Wiley & Sons; London: Chapman & Hall.
why: Laplace independently rebuilt and generalized Bayes's result, and this non-technical essay is where he lays out probability as "common sense reduced to calculation." It covers inverse probability (the probability of causes), the principle of insufficient reason, and his famous deterministic "intelligence" (later called Laplace's demon). It is the bridge between Bayes's narrow problem and the modern view of probability as reasoning under ignorance.

strand: Foundations — probability as extended logic, history, subjective probability
citation: Cox, R. T. (1946). *Probability, Frequency and Reasonable Expectation*. American Journal of Physics, 14(1), 1–13. DOI: 10.1119/1.1990764
why: Cox shows that any system for grading degrees of plausibility that meets a few common-sense consistency requirements has to obey the sum and product rules of probability. This is "Cox's theorem," the formal backbone of the view that Bayesian probability is the unique extension of logic to uncertainty. Jaynes's Chapter 2 rebuilds the argument, so read Cox for the original and Jaynes for the exposition.

strand: Foundations — probability as extended logic, history, subjective probability
citation: Jaynes, E. T. (2003). *Probability Theory: The Logic of Science* (G. L. Bretthorst, Ed.). Cambridge University Press.
why: This is the most forceful statement of probability as extended logic. Jaynes imagines building a "reasoning robot," derives the rules of probability from desiderata of consistency, and then uses them to handle sampling, hypothesis testing, maximum-entropy priors and model comparison. It is polemical against "orthodox" statistics in a way that sharpens your intuition even where you disagree.
focus: Ch. 1 Plausible reasoning; Ch. 2 The quantitative rules; Ch. 4 Elementary hypothesis testing; Ch. 5 Queer uses for probability theory; Ch. 11 Discrete prior probabilities: the entropy principle; Ch. 17 Principles and pathology of orthodox statistics; Ch. 20 Model comparison

strand: Foundations — probability as extended logic, history, subjective probability
citation: McGrayne, S. B. (2011). *The Theory That Would Not Die: How Bayes' Rule Cracked the Enigma Code, Hunted Down Russian Submarines, and Emerged Triumphant from Two Centuries of Controversy*. New Haven: Yale University Press.
why: This is the accessible on-ramp: a narrative history of Bayes's rule from Bayes and Laplace, through its banishment by the frequentists, to codebreaking, actuarial work, submarine search and modern computing. It explains why the debate became so heated and gives every later technical text a human context. Read it first.
translation: 『異端の統計学 ベイズ』 シャロン・バーチュ・マグレイン著, 冨永星訳, 草思社 (2013; 草思社文庫版 2018)

strand: Foundations — probability as extended logic, history, subjective probability
citation: Hájek, A. (2002; substantive revision 2023). *Interpretations of Probability*. In E. N. Zalta & U. Nodelman (Eds.), *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*.
why: This is the authoritative map of what "probability" can mean: classical, logical, subjective, frequency, propensity and best-system interpretations. It is the best legal free entry point to de Finetti's subjectivism and the Dutch Book argument, which says incoherent betting odds can be exploited for a sure loss. It also places Jaynes's objective Bayesianism in context.
focus: §3.2 Logical/Evidential Probability; §3.3 Subjective Interpretation (esp. 3.3.2 The betting analysis and the Dutch Book argument; 3.3.5 Objective Bayesianism); §3.4 Frequency Interpretations

strand: Debates — frequentist vs Bayesian, and what Bayesian practice really is
citation: Efron, B. (1986). *Why Isn't Everyone a Bayesian?* The American Statistician, 40(1), 1–5. DOI: 10.1080/00031305.1986.10475342
why: One of the twentieth century's leading statisticians, and the inventor of the bootstrap, explains in five pages why Bayesian theory's coherence had not won over practitioners. His reasons include the difficulty of specifying priors, the appeal of "objective" procedures, and the convenience of frequentist tools. It is the classic short statement of the case for pragmatic frequentism. Read it alongside Jaynes's polemics and Gelman & Shalizi's reconciliation.

strand: Debates — frequentist vs Bayesian, and what Bayesian practice really is
citation: Gelman, A., & Shalizi, C. R. (2013). *Philosophy and the Practice of Bayesian Statistics*. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 66(1), 8–38. DOI: 10.1111/j.2044-8317.2011.02037.x
why: The paper argues that successful Bayesian practice is not inductive "belief updating" but hypothetico-deductive: you fit a model, check it against data, and revise it, which is closer to Popper (and to Mayo's error statistics) than to subjectivism. It is essential for a social scientist who wants a defensible philosophy behind posterior predictive checks and model revision.

citation: Johnson, A. A., Ott, M. Q., & Dogucu, M. (2022). *Bayes Rules! An Introduction to Applied Bayesian Modeling*. Chapman & Hall/CRC. DOI: 10.1201/9780429288340
why: This is the gentlest rigorous on-ramp, written for undergraduates. It moves from Bayes' rule for events, through conjugate Beta-Binomial models and MCMC "under the hood," to regression and hierarchical models. It was a required text alongside McElreath in the Georgia State syllabus used for triangulation. The full text is free online.
focus: Part I Bayesian Foundations (Ch. 1–5); Ch. 7 MCMC under the Hood; Part IV Hierarchical Bayesian Models (Ch. 15–17)

citation: McElreath, R. (2020). *Statistical Rethinking: A Bayesian Course with Examples in R and Stan* (2nd ed.). Chapman & Hall/CRC. DOI: 10.1201/9780429029608
why: This is the best book for building modeling intuition. It treats models as "golems," builds everything from simulation, and weaves causal DAGs into regression from the start, so confounding, colliders and post-treatment bias are part of the Bayesian workflow and not an afterthought. The free 20-lecture video course (CC0 materials) is canonical in its own right, and there are community translations of the code into Python (PyMC, NumPyro).
focus: Ch. 1 The Golem of Prague; Ch. 2 Small Worlds and Large Worlds; Ch. 4 Geocentric Models; Ch. 5 The Many Variables & The Spurious Waffles; Ch. 6 The Haunted DAG & The Causal Terror; Ch. 7 Ulysses' Compass; Ch. 9 Markov Chain Monte Carlo; Ch. 13 Models With Memory; Ch. 14 Adventures in Covariance
access: need-copy (book). Free sample Ch. 1–2: https://xcelab.net/rmpubs/sr2/statisticalrethinking2_chapters1and2.pdf. Free lectures, slides and homework: https://github.com/rmcelreath/stat_rethinking_2024

citation: Gelman, A., Carlin, J. B., Stern, H. S., Dunson, D. B., Vehtari, A., & Rubin, D. B. (2013). *Bayesian Data Analysis* (3rd ed.). Chapman & Hall/CRC. DOI: 10.1201/b16018
why: This is the standard graduate reference for applied Bayesian statistics. It codifies the "three steps" (build a full probability model, condition on data, evaluate fit) and makes hierarchical (multilevel) models and posterior predictive checking central. Its later chapters are the reference for computation, regression, missing data, Gaussian processes and mixtures. The authors post a free PDF for non-commercial use.
focus: Ch. 1 Probability and inference; Ch. 2 Single-parameter models; Ch. 5 Hierarchical models; Ch. 6 Model checking; Ch. 7 Evaluating, comparing, and expanding models; Ch. 8 Modeling accounting for data collection; Ch. 11 Basics of Markov chain simulation

citation: Gelman, A., Vehtari, A., Simpson, D., Margossian, C. C., Carpenter, B., Yao, Y., Kennedy, L., Gabry, J., Bürkner, P.-C., & Modrák, M. (2020). *Bayesian Workflow*. arXiv:2011.01808.
why: The paper reframes Bayesian statistics from "compute the posterior" to an iterative process: prior predictive checks, fake-data simulation, computational diagnostics, model expansion and comparison, and dealing with many models at once. It is the modern statement of how Stan-era practitioners actually work, and the most directly useful item for Kunhao's own empirical modeling.

citation: Robert, C., & Casella, G. (2011). *A Short History of Markov Chain Monte Carlo: Subjective Recollections from Incomplete Data*. Statistical Science, 26(1), 102–115. DOI: 10.1214/10-STS351
why: The paper traces MCMC from the 1953 Metropolis algorithm at Los Alamos, through Hastings and the Gibbs sampler, to the 1990 Gelfand–Smith paper that turned Bayesian statistics into a practical discipline. It is the best single guide to the primary computational papers and shows why computation, more than philosophy, ended the Bayesian "winter."

citation: Betancourt, M. (2017). *A Conceptual Introduction to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo*. arXiv:1701.02434 (v2, 2018).
why: This is the clearest geometric explanation of why random-walk samplers fail in high dimensions (concentration of measure and the "typical set") and how Hamiltonian dynamics let a sampler glide along that set. HMC/NUTS is the engine inside Stan and PyMC, and this paper turns divergences and other diagnostics from mysterious warnings into interpretable signals.

citation: Blei, D. M., Kucukelbir, A., & McAuliffe, J. D. (2017). *Variational Inference: A Review for Statisticians*. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 112(518), 859–877. DOI: 10.1080/01621459.2017.1285773
why: The review explains the alternative to sampling: turn inference into optimization by finding the member of a tractable family closest (in KL divergence) to the posterior, which means maximizing the ELBO. It covers mean-field coordinate ascent and stochastic VI, and it is the conceptual link to topic models, VAEs and much of modern probabilistic deep learning.

citation: MacKay, D. J. C. (2003). *Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms*. Cambridge University Press.
why: A physicist's unification of information theory, Bayesian inference and neural networks, with famously intuitive exercises. Its treatment of the Bayesian Occam's razor (why the marginal likelihood automatically penalizes over-flexible models) and its Monte Carlo and variational chapters are classics. It is the natural bridge text to the AI4Read information-theory canon. CUP allows free on-screen viewing of the PDF.
focus: Ch. 2 Probability, Entropy, and Inference; Ch. 3 More about Inference; Ch. 28 Model Comparison and Occam's Razor; Monte Carlo Methods (Ch. 29); Ch. 30 Efficient Monte Carlo Methods; Ch. 33 Variational Methods; Ch. 37 Bayesian Inference and Sampling Theory
verified: https://www.inference.org.uk/itprnn/book.pdf (title page: "Cambridge University Press 2003. On-screen viewing permitted.")

citation: Murphy, K. P. (2023). *Probabilistic Machine Learning: Advanced Topics*. MIT Press.
why: This is the encyclopedic modern reference connecting Bayesian inference to machine learning. It has chapters on inference algorithms, variational inference, MCMC, Bayesian neural networks, generative models and causality, all in one consistent notation with Python (JAX) code. Use it as a lookup, not a cover-to-cover read. The author posts a free draft PDF (CC BY-NC-ND).
focus: Ch. 7 Inference algorithms: an overview; Ch. 10 Variational inference; Ch. 12 Markov chain Monte Carlo; Ch. 36 Causality

citation: Griffiths, T. L., & Tenenbaum, J. B. (2006). *Optimal Predictions in Everyday Cognition*. Psychological Science, 17(9), 767–773. DOI: 10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01780.x
why: People were asked to predict totals from partial information, such as a movie's final gross from its earnings so far or a man's lifespan from his current age. Their median predictions closely matched optimal Bayesian predictions under the real-world prior distributions. This is the cleanest demonstration that everyday intuition embodies accurate priors, and that the form of the prior (power-law vs Gaussian vs Erlang) shapes judgment.

citation: Tenenbaum, J. B., Kemp, C., Griffiths, T. L., & Goodman, N. D. (2011). *How to Grow a Mind: Statistics, Structure, and Abstraction*. Science, 331(6022), 1279–1285. DOI: 10.1126/science.1192788
why: This is the manifesto of the "reverse-engineering" program. It asks how minds learn so much from so little data and answers with Bayesian inference over structured representations (graphs, grammars, programs), hierarchical models that learn their own priors ("learning to learn"), and nonparametric models that grow in complexity. It is the opening reading of MIT 9.660.

citation: Griffiths, T. L., Chater, N., & Tenenbaum, J. B. (2024). *Bayesian Models of Cognition: Reverse Engineering the Mind*. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 9780262049412.
why: This is the field's definitive textbook, written by its three leading figures. Part I builds up the mathematics (Bayesian inference, graphical models, hierarchical and nonparametric models, sampling) with psychological examples. Part II covers advanced applications and also critiques of the reverse-engineering approach. It consolidates two decades of papers into one coherent framework.
focus: Part I (core mathematical ideas); then Part II selectively, including the critique chapters

citation: Rubin, D. B. (1974). *Estimating Causal Effects of Treatments in Randomized and Nonrandomized Studies*. Journal of Educational Psychology, 66(5), 688–701. DOI: 10.1037/h0037350
why: This is the founding paper of the modern potential-outcomes framework, often called the Rubin Causal Model. A causal effect is defined as the difference between the outcomes a unit would have under treatment and under control, and the paper asks when nonrandomized data can still estimate it. Everything in Imbens & Rubin and Hernán & Robins builds on this definition.

citation: Holland, P. W. (1986). *Statistics and Causal Inference*. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 81(396), 945–960. DOI: 10.1080/01621459.1986.10478354
why: This is the canonical exposition of the potential-outcomes view. It names the "Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference" (we never observe both potential outcomes for the same unit) and popularizes the slogan "no causation without manipulation." It contrasts this view with philosophical accounts of causation and is required reading in Berkeley's Stat 256.

citation: Pearl, J. (2009). *Causality: Models, Reasoning, and Inference* (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press. DOI: 10.1017/CBO9780511803161
why: This is the treatise behind structural causal models. It covers causal Bayesian networks, d-separation, the do-operator and do-calculus, identification criteria (back-door and front-door), structural counterfactuals and the probability of causation. It won the 2001 Lakatos Award, and it is the mathematical source for everything popularized in the Primer and *The Book of Why*.
focus: Ch. 1 Introduction to Probabilities, Graphs, and Causal Models; Ch. 3 Causal Diagrams and the Identification of Causal Effects; Ch. 5 Causality and Structural Models in Social Science and Economics; Ch. 6 Simpson's Paradox, Confounding, and Collapsibility; Ch. 7 The Logic of Structure-Based Counterfactuals; Epilogue "The Art and Science of Cause and Effect"
translation: 『統計的因果推論 ―モデル・推論・推測―』 黒木学訳, 共立出版 (2009) — a translation of the 1st edition (2000)

citation: Pearl, J., Glymour, M., & Jewell, N. P. (2016). *Causal Inference in Statistics: A Primer*. Chichester: Wiley.
why: This is the compact (about 130-page) textbook version of Pearl's framework, written for students who know basic statistics. It covers Simpson's paradox, chains, forks and colliders, d-separation, interventions and the adjustment formula, the back-door and front-door criteria, mediation and counterfactuals, with exercises. It is the fastest route to working fluency with DAGs.
focus: whole (4 chapters): Ch. 1 Preliminaries: Statistical and Causal Models; Ch. 2 Graphical Models and Their Applications; Ch. 3 The Effects of Interventions; Ch. 4 Counterfactuals and Their Applications
access: need-copy (the author posts Ch. 1–2 in full: https://bayes.cs.ucla.edu/PRIMER/primer-ch1.pdf, https://bayes.cs.ucla.edu/PRIMER/primer-ch2.pdf)
translation: 『入門 統計的因果推論』 落海浩訳, 朝倉書店 (2019)

citation: Pearl, J., & Mackenzie, D. (2018). *The Book of Why: The New Science of Cause and Effect*. New York: Basic Books.
why: This is the popular on-ramp to causal inference. Its organizing idea is the "Ladder of Causation" (association → intervention → counterfactuals): data alone cannot climb the ladder without a causal model. The book also tells the history of path analysis, the smoking–cancer controversy and causal paradoxes, so it gives strong intuitions before the formal Primer. It is opinionated about statistics' history, so read it with Holland and Imbens & Rubin as a counterweight.
translation: 『因果推論の科学 「なぜ?」の問いにどう答えるか』 夏目大訳, 松尾豊監修・解説, 文藝春秋 (2022)
verified: https://bayes.cs.ucla.edu/WHY/ (JP: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/ジューディア・パール)

citation: Imbens, G. W., & Rubin, D. B. (2015). *Causal Inference for Statistics, Social, and Biomedical Sciences: An Introduction*. Cambridge University Press. DOI: 10.1017/CBO9781139025751
why: This is the definitive potential-outcomes textbook. It is built around assignment mechanisms: randomized experiments analyzed via Fisher, Neyman, regression and Bayesian model-based approaches, then observational studies under unconfoundedness with propensity scores, overlap, matching and trimming. Pearl's framework starts from graphs; this one starts from the design of the study. Imbens shared the 2021 economics Nobel for this tradition.
focus: Part I (Ch. 1 Causality: The Basic Framework; Ch. 2 A Brief History of the Potential Outcomes Approach; Ch. 3 A Classification of Assignment Mechanisms); Ch. 5 Fisher's Exact P-Values; Ch. 6 Neyman's Repeated Sampling Approach; Ch. 8 Model-Based Inference; Ch. 12 Unconfounded Treatment Assignment; Ch. 13 Estimating the Propensity Score

citation: Hernán, M. A., & Robins, J. M. (2020). *Causal Inference: What If*. Boca Raton: Chapman & Hall/CRC.
why: This is the clearest modern textbook that unifies potential outcomes with causal DAGs. It moves from the definition of a causal effect through confounding, selection and measurement bias, to IP weighting, the g-formula, g-estimation and time-varying treatments. Its "target trial emulation" idea (design the observational analysis as if it were a randomized trial) is now standard practice. The authors keep it free and updated online, and it is a core text at Berkeley.
focus: Part I Causal inference without models (Ch. 1 A definition of causal effect through Ch. 10, esp. Ch. 6 Graphical representation of causal effects; Ch. 7 Confounding; Ch. 8 Selection bias); Part II Ch. 12 IP weighting and marginal structural models; Ch. 13 Standardization and the parametric g-formula; Part III Ch. 22 Target trial emulation
access: free: https://miguelhernan.org/s/hernanrobins_WhatIf_19aug26.pdf (the link changes with each revision; landing page https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook)

citation: Morgan, S. L., & Winship, C. (2014). *Counterfactuals and Causal Inference: Methods and Principles for Social Research* (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press, Analytical Methods for Social Research. DOI: 10.1017/CBO9781107587991 (often cited as 2015)
why: This is the causal-inference synthesis written by and for sociologists. It uses both potential outcomes and causal graphs, then covers matching, regression, weighting, instrumental variables, mechanisms, panel data and partial identification, with social-science examples throughout. It is the closest fit to Kunhao's own disciplinary audience and the best guide to what regression coefficients in observational social research do and don't mean.
focus: Ch. 1 Introduction; Ch. 2 Counterfactuals and the Potential Outcome Model; Ch. 3 Causal Graphs; Ch. 4 Models of Causal Exposure and Identification Criteria for Conditioning Estimators; Ch. 6 Regression Estimators of Causal Effects; Ch. 10 Mechanisms and Causal Explanation

citation: Craig, R. T. (1999). Communication Theory as a Field. *Communication Theory*, 9(2), 119–161. DOI: 10.1111/j.1468-2885.1999.tb00355.x
why: Craig argues that communication theory is a "practical discipline": a dialogue among seven traditions (rhetorical, semiotic, phenomenological, cybernetic, sociopsychological, sociocultural, critical), each of which defines communication differently and so sees different problems. It is the most widely used map of the field, and it shows which tradition a given theory or paper speaks from.

citation: Craig, R. T., & Muller, H. L. (Eds.) (2007). *Theorizing Communication: Readings Across Traditions*. SAGE. ISBN 9781412952378.
why: An anthology built on Craig's 1999 map, with one unit per tradition. Each unit pairs primary sources (Saussure, Peirce, Buber, Gadamer, Watzlawick, Mead, Marx, Horkheimer and Adorno, Habermas) with an editors' introduction. It is the best single overview text for seeing the whole field through its original voices.
focus: Unit II (ch. 5, "Communication Theory as a Field"); Unit I ch. 4 "A Cultural Approach to Communication"; Unit VI "The Cybernetic Tradition" (ch. 19–22); Unit IX "The Critical Tradition" (ch. 31–35)

citation: Shannon, C. E., & Weaver, W. (1949). *The Mathematical Theory of Communication*. University of Illinois Press. Contains Shannon's paper (from *Bell System Technical Journal*, 27, 379–423, 623–656, 1948) and Weaver's essay "Recent contributions to the mathematical theory of communication".
why: This book is the source of the "transmission model" (source, transmitter, channel and noise, receiver), the most influential and most criticized picture of communication. Shannon defines information as reduction of uncertainty and deliberately sets meaning aside. Weaver's essay then speculates about "semantic" and "effectiveness" levels, and that speculation is what social scientists took up. You need to read both to see what communication theory borrowed from engineering and what it misread.
focus: Weaver's essay (whole); Shannon's Introduction and Part I "Discrete Noiseless Systems", especially §2 "The Discrete Source of Information" and §3 "The Series of Approximations to English"
access: free: https://people.math.harvard.edu/~ctm/home/text/others/shannon/entropy/entropy.pdf (Shannon's paper only; Weaver's essay is need-copy)
translation: 『通信の数学的理論』植松友彦訳, ちくま学芸文庫(筑摩書房), 2009

citation: Wiener, N. (1948/2019). *Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine*. MIT Press (2nd ed. 1961; MIT Press reissue 2019, ISBN 9780262537841).
why: Wiener defines communication as control through feedback, the same in machines, organisms and societies. This is the root of Craig's "cybernetic tradition" and of systems thinking in Luhmann and in social simulation. Much of the book is technical mathematics, so read it for the framing ideas rather than cover to cover.
translation: 『サイバネティックス――動物と機械における制御と通信』池原止戈夫・弥永昌吉・室賀三郎訳, 岩波書店, 2011

citation: Lasswell, H. D. (1948). The Structure and Function of Communication in Society. In L. Bryson (Ed.), *The Communication of Ideas* (pp. 37–51). Institute for Religious and Social Studies / Harper & Brothers.
why: Source of the formula "Who says what in which channel to whom with what effect?", which divided early mass communication research into control, content, media, audience and effects analysis. It also gives a functionalist account of what communication does for a society. It is short, and it explains why the field came to be organized around effects.

citation: Lippmann, W. (1922). *Public Opinion*. Harcourt, Brace. (Project Gutenberg eBook #6456.)
why: People act on "pictures in their heads" (a pseudo-environment) rather than on the world itself, and the press and stereotypes build those pictures. The book anticipates agenda setting, framing and the problem of democratic competence a generation before these were tested empirically. It is the origin text of public-opinion and media-effects thinking.
focus: Part I, ch. I "The World Outside and the Pictures in Our Heads"; Part III "Stereotypes" (ch. VI–X); Part VII "Newspapers", especially ch. XXIII "The Nature of News"
translation: 『世論』(上・下) 掛川トミ子訳, 岩波文庫, 1987

citation: Katz, E., & Lazarsfeld, P. F. (1955). *Personal Influence: The Part Played by People in the Flow of Mass Communications*. Free Press. (Transaction re-issue 2005/2006 with a new preface by Katz.)
why: The Decatur study puts the two-step flow and opinion leaders at the centre of the limited-effects paradigm: media messages are filtered through primary groups and interpersonal networks. It is the founding bridge between media effects and network science, and it is still the reference point for debates about influencers and one-step flow.
focus: Ch. 1; Katz's 2006 preface "Lazarsfeld's Legacy: The Power of Limited Effects" (pp. xv–xxvii)

citation: McCombs, M. E., & Shaw, D. L. (1972). The Agenda-Setting Function of Mass Media. *Public Opinion Quarterly*, 36(2), 176–187. DOI: 10.1086/267990
why: The Chapel Hill study shows that the issues the media emphasize become the issues voters consider important ("what to think about", not "what to think"). It reopened the case for strong cognitive media effects, and it set the template for a design you can compute directly: content salience against public salience.

citation: Entman, R. M. (1993). Framing: Toward Clarification of a Fractured Paradigm. *Journal of Communication*, 43(4), 51–58. DOI: 10.1111/j.1460-2466.1993.tb01304.x
why: Entman gives the standard working definition of framing: selecting and making salient some aspects of a perceived reality so as to promote a problem definition, a causal interpretation, a moral evaluation and a treatment recommendation. Most computational frame-detection codebooks still use these four functions.

citation: Goffman, E. (1974). *Frame Analysis: An Essay on the Organization of Experience*. (Northeastern University Press edition, ISBN 0-930350-91-X.)
why: The sociological source of "frame": the interpretive schemata (primary frameworks, natural and social) that answer "what is going on here?". Media framing research borrowed the word but mostly dropped Goffman's micro-sociology. Reading him shows what that borrowing lost and gives the theory more depth.

citation: Noelle-Neumann, E. (1974). The Spiral of Silence: A Theory of Public Opinion. *Journal of Communication*, 24(2), 43–51. DOI: 10.1111/j.1460-2466.1974.tb00367.x
why: People fear isolation and use a "quasi-statistical sense" to read the climate of opinion. Those who think they are in the minority fall silent, which makes the majority look larger still, so the process feeds on itself. The result is a dynamic, feedback-driven theory of opinion that maps directly onto agent-based simulation and onto self-censorship online.

citation: Gerbner, G., & Gross, L. (1976). Living with Television: The Violence Profile. *Journal of Communication*, 26(2), 172–199. DOI: 10.1111/j.1460-2466.1976.tb01397.x
why: The founding statement of cultivation theory. Long-term, cumulative exposure to television's consistent symbolic world shapes viewers' beliefs about social reality: heavy viewers give the "television answer" and see a meaner, more dangerous world. It is the model for effects that are slow, diffuse and found at the level of the whole system.

citation: Katz, E., Blumler, J. G., & Gurevitch, M. (1973). Uses and Gratifications Research. *Public Opinion Quarterly*, 37(4), 509–523. DOI: 10.1086/268109
why: It turns the effects question around, from "what do media do to people?" to "what do people do with media?". It sets out the assumptions of the active-audience approach: social and psychological needs produce expectations, which produce media selection and gratifications. Selective-exposure and platform-choice research descends from this paper.

citation: Scheufele, D. A., & Tewksbury, D. (2007). Framing, Agenda Setting, and Priming: The Evolution of Three Media Effects Models. *Journal of Communication*, 57(1), 9–20. DOI: 10.1111/j.0021-9916.2007.00326.x
why: It separates the three main cognitive-effects models by mechanism. Agenda setting and priming work through accessibility (what is salient in memory); framing works through applicability (which interpretive schema a message invokes). It is the conceptual hygiene needed before you operationalize any of the three.

citation: Bennett, W. L., & Iyengar, S. (2008). A New Era of Minimal Effects? The Changing Foundations of Political Communication. *Journal of Communication*, 58(4), 707–731. DOI: 10.1111/j.1460-2466.2008.00410.x
why: Audience fragmentation and partisan selective exposure in a high-choice media environment may bring back "minimal effects", now for structural reasons (reinforcement, preaching to the converted) rather than because of interpersonal filtering. It started a major debate (see Holbert et al.'s reply in the same journal) on whether the mid-century theories still hold.

citation: Rogers, E. M. (2003). *Diffusion of Innovations* (5th ed.). Free Press. ISBN 0743222091.
why: It synthesizes thousands of diffusion studies into one framework: innovation attributes, communication channels, time and the social system. It explains the S-curve, adopter categories, opinion leaders, homophily and heterophily, and critical mass. It is the canonical bridge from communication to epidemiology-style and network-contagion models.

citation: Centola, D., & Macy, M. (2007). Complex Contagions and the Weakness of Long Ties. *American Journal of Sociology*, 113(3), 702–734. DOI: 10.1086/521848
why: For behaviours that need reinforcement from several contacts (complex contagions), the long "weak ties" that speed up simple information diffusion (Granovetter) can slow spread, and clustered, wide bridges matter instead. It updates two-step-flow and diffusion thinking with formal network models. The experimental follow-up is Centola (2010), *Science*, 329, 1194–1197.

citation: Habermas, J. (1962/1989). *The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere: An Inquiry into a Category of Bourgeois Society* (T. Burger, Trans.). MIT Press.
why: A historical-normative account of how a reasoning public of private persons arose in eighteenth-century coffeehouses, salons and the press. It then argues that this public sphere was "refeudalized" by commercial mass media, PR and the welfare state. It is the normative yardstick behind nearly every argument about deliberation, polarization and platform governance.
translation: 『公共性の構造転換』未來社, 1973 (第2版 1994)

citation: Carey, J. W. (1989). A Cultural Approach to Communication. In *Communication as Culture: Essays on Media and Society*. Unwin Hyman / Routledge (essay orig. 1975). Reprinted as ch. 4 in Craig & Muller (2007).
why: It contrasts the "transmission view" (sending messages across space for control) with a "ritual view" (communication as the sustaining of shared beliefs and community over time). It is the best short antidote to treating communication only as information transfer, and it explains why sharing misinformation can work as identity ritual rather than as belief.
focus: the essay "A Cultural Approach to Communication" (whole)

citation: Hall, S. (1973). *Encoding and Decoding in the Television Discourse*. CCCS Stencilled Occasional Paper No. 7. Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies, University of Birmingham. (Revised as "Encoding/decoding" in Hall et al. (Eds.), *Culture, Media, Language*, Hutchinson, 1980, pp. 128–137.)
why: Meaning is not transmitted intact. Producers encode it under institutional codes, and audiences decode it from social positions, which yields dominant-hegemonic, negotiated or oppositional readings of a "preferred reading". It is the cultural-studies answer to Shannon and Lasswell, and the basis of active-audience research on polarized interpretation.

citation: Luhmann, N. (2000). *The Reality of the Mass Media* (K. Cross, Trans.). Stanford University Press. (German orig. *Die Realität der Massenmedien*, 1996.)
why: A systems-theory account of mass media as a self-referential (autopoietic) social system that runs on the code information/non-information. "Whatever we know about our society, or indeed about the world in which we live, we know through the mass media." It is a short, demanding, non-normative counterweight to Habermas, and a natural fit for second-order cybernetic and simulation thinking.
translation: 『マスメディアのリアリティ』木鐸社, 2005

citation: McLuhan, M. (1964/1994). *Understanding Media: The Extensions of Man*. McGraw-Hill (1964); MIT Press ed. 1994 with an introduction by L. H. Lapham.
why: "The medium is the message": the structural properties of a medium reshape perception and social organization more than any content it carries. It is the founding text of medium theory (with Innis), aphoristic and uneven, but it is the source of questions about what platforms and LLM interfaces do independent of content.
translation: 『メディア論――人間の拡張の諸相』

citation: Kasperson, R. E., Renn, O., Slovic, P., Brown, H. S., Emel, J., Goble, R., et al. (1988). The Social Amplification of Risk: A Conceptual Framework. *Risk Analysis*, 8(2), 177–187. DOI: 10.1111/j.1539-6924.1988.tb01168.x
why: The social amplification of risk framework (SARF) borrows the signal-amplification metaphor from information theory. Risk signals pass through "amplification stations" (media, experts, groups), which magnify or dampen them and produce secondary "ripple" impacts far beyond the physical hazard. It is the integrating framework for crisis and risk communication and links directly to Kunhao's heatwave and climate work.
access: free: https://doi.org/10.18419/opus-7221 (submitted version in the University of Stuttgart OPUS repository, as indexed by OpenAlex; the repository's bot check blocked direct inspection, so the file was not opened)

citation: Slovic, P. (1987). Perception of Risk. *Science*, 236(4799), 280–285. DOI: 10.1126/science.3563507
why: The psychometric paradigm. Lay risk judgments are organized along "dread" and "unknown" factors rather than expected fatalities, which explains the systematic gaps between expert and public risk rankings. It is essential for understanding why risk messages fail and why some hazards act as "signal" events.
access: free: https://scholarsbank.uoregon.edu/bitstreams/0439bd1c-eca4-4e9e-95b7-3082de3bc55b/download (author manuscript, Univ. of Oregon repository)

citation: Coombs, W. T. (2007). Protecting Organization Reputations During a Crisis: The Development and Application of Situational Crisis Communication Theory. *Corporate Reputation Review*, 10(3), 163–176. DOI: 10.1057/palgrave.crr.1550049
why: Situational Crisis Communication Theory (SCCT) applies attribution theory to crises. Stakeholders' attributions of crisis responsibility (shaped by crisis type, crisis history and prior reputation) determine reputational threat, and response strategies (deny, diminish, rebuild, bolster) should be matched to that threat. It is the dominant evidence-based theory of organizational crisis response.

citation: Vosoughi, S., Roy, D., & Aral, S. (2018). The spread of true and false news online. *Science*, 359(6380), 1146–1151. DOI: 10.1126/science.aap9559
why: Using all fact-checked rumour cascades on Twitter from 2006 to 2017, the paper finds that falsehood diffused farther, faster, deeper and more broadly than truth, and that humans rather than bots drove the difference. The authors propose a novelty and emotion account. It is the landmark computational study tying diffusion-network metrics (cascade depth, breadth, structural virality) to misinformation.
focus: whole (with supplementary materials for the cascade metrics)

citation: Lazer, D. M. J., Baum, M. A., Benkler, Y., Berinsky, A. J., Greenhill, K. M., Menczer, F., Metzger, M. J., Nyhan, B., et al. (2018). The science of fake news. *Science*, 359(6380), 1094–1096. DOI: 10.1126/science.aao2998
why: A short interdisciplinary agenda-setting statement. It defines fake news as fabricated information that mimics news-media content in form but not in organizational process or intent. It frames the problem as a joint failure of individuals and platforms, and it sets out the research and intervention agenda that much later computational work followed.

citation: Lewandowsky, S., Ecker, U. K. H., Seifert, C. M., Schwarz, N., & Cook, J. (2012). Misinformation and Its Correction: Continued Influence and Successful Debiasing. *Psychological Science in the Public Interest*, 13(3), 106–131. DOI: 10.1177/1529100612451018
why: The canonical cognitive review of why retractions fail. Misinformation keeps influencing reasoning even after it is corrected (the continued influence effect) because corrections leave gaps in people's mental models, and familiarity, overkill and worldview pressures add to this. The review also shows what works: warnings, repetition of the correction, and alternative causal explanations. Later work has substantially qualified the "backfire" claims, so read it alongside newer replications.

citation: Weaver, W. (1948). *Science and Complexity*. American Scientist, 36, 536 ff. (adapted from ch. 1 of *The Scientists Speak*, 1947). Reprinted in Krakauer (ed.), *Foundational Papers in Complexity Science*, Vol. 1 (SFI Press, 2024).
why: The founding taxonomy: problems of simplicity (few variables), of disorganized complexity (many variables, tamed by statistics), and of organized complexity (many interacting variables that are neither). Almost every later definition of a "complex system" is a refinement of Weaver's middle ground, and it reads in under an hour.

citation: Simon, H. A. (1962). *The Architecture of Complexity*. Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society, 106(6), 467–482. JSTOR 985254.
why: Argues that complex systems tend to be hierarchic and "nearly decomposable": strong interactions within subsystems, weak ones between them. The watchmaker parable (Tempus vs. Hora) explains why stable intermediate forms make evolution of complexity fast. This is the conceptual root of modularity, community structure and multi-scale modeling.
focus: whole (the watchmaker parable and the near-decomposability section are the essentials)

citation: Anderson, P. W. (1972). *More Is Different*. Science, 177(4047), 393–396. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.177.4047.393
why: A Nobel physicist's manifesto against naive constructionism: reductionism can be true while "reconstructing the universe from the laws" fails, because broken symmetry creates new levels with their own laws. It is the standard citation for emergence as a scientific (not mystical) claim.

citation: Mitchell, M. (2009). *Complexity: A Guided Tour*. Oxford University Press.
why: The best single on-ramp to the whole field, written by an SFI researcher, covering dynamics/chaos, information, computation, evolution, cellular automata, networks and scaling in plain language. It also surveys the competing definitions of complexity, so the reader learns that the field has no single definition.
focus: Part One "Background and History" (What is complexity?; Dynamics, chaos, and prediction; Information; Computation; Defining and measuring complexity); "Cellular automata, life, and the universe"; Part Four "Network Thinking" (The mystery of scaling); Conclusion "The past and future of the sciences of complexity"
translation: 『ガイドツアー 複雑系の世界：サンタフェ研究所講義ノートから』メラニー・ミッチェル著、高橋洋訳、紀伊國屋書店

citation: Ladyman, J., Lambert, J., & Wiesner, K. (2013). *What is a complex system?* European Journal for Philosophy of Science, 3(1), 33–67. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13194-012-0056-8
why: A philosophy-of-science audit of the many definitions of complexity, separating necessary from merely typical features (many interacting elements, disorder, robustness, emergence, hierarchy, memory, nonlinearity, feedback) and reviewing quantitative complexity measures. It is the go-to reference for writing a defensible definition in a paper.

citation: Strogatz, S. H. (2024). *Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos: With Applications to Physics, Biology, Chemistry, and Engineering* (3rd ed.). Chapman & Hall/CRC Press. (2nd ed. 2015 is equally usable.)
why: The standard textbook for building geometric intuition about fixed points, stability, bifurcations, limit cycles and chaos, with applications drawn from many sciences. Almost every tipping-point or opinion-dynamics argument in social science silently relies on concepts taught in its first eight chapters.
focus: Ch. 2 Flows on the Line; Ch. 3 Bifurcations; Ch. 5 Linear Systems; Ch. 6 Phase Plane; Ch. 8 Bifurcations Revisited; Ch. 9 Lorenz Equations; Ch. 10 One-Dimensional Maps; Ch. 13 Kuramoto Model (new in 3rd ed.)
translation: 『ストロガッツ 非線形ダイナミクスとカオス：数学的基礎から物理・生物・化学・工学への応用まで』丸善出版（2015年頃、旧版の翻訳）

citation: May, R. M. (1976). *Simple mathematical models with very complicated dynamics*. Nature, 261(5560), 459–467. https://doi.org/10.1038/261459a0
why: Shows that the one-line logistic difference equation passes through period-doubling into chaos, and pleads that every student meet it early. It is the canonical demonstration that deterministic simplicity does not imply predictable behavior, which is the lesson behind all "simple rules, complex outcomes" claims in social modeling.

citation: Lorenz, E. N. (1963). *Deterministic Nonperiodic Flow*. Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences, 20(2), 130–141. https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0469(1963)020<0130:DNF>2.0.CO;2
why: The original discovery of sensitive dependence on initial conditions in a three-variable convection model (the Lorenz attractor). Read it after Strogatz Ch. 9 for the historical source of "chaos" and the limits of prediction.
focus: whole (skim the derivation; focus on the numerical results and the discussion of predictability)

strand: Emergence in social systems and agent-based models
citation: Schelling, T. C. (1971). *Dynamic models of segregation*. Journal of Mathematical Sociology, 1(2), 143–186. https://doi.org/10.1080/0022250X.1971.9989794
why: The paradigm case of emergence in social science: mild individual preferences about neighbors produce stark macro segregation that nobody intended. It also introduced tipping and the "micromotives vs. macrobehavior" framing that defines agent-based social science. (The book-length treatment is Schelling's *Micromotives and Macrobehavior*, 1978.)

strand: Emergence in social systems and agent-based models
citation: Granovetter, M. (1978). *Threshold Models of Collective Behavior*. American Journal of Sociology, 83(6), 1420–1443. https://doi.org/10.1086/226707
why: Models each person as having a threshold (how many others must act before they do) and shows that the distribution of thresholds, not average preferences, decides whether a riot or adoption cascade happens. Small changes to one person's threshold can flip the collective outcome, which is the core intuition behind cascade and misinformation-spread models.

strand: Emergence in social systems and agent-based models
citation: Epstein, J. M., & Axtell, R. L. (1996). *Growing Artificial Societies: Social Science from the Bottom Up*. Brookings Institution Press / MIT Press. 228 pp.
why: The Sugarscape book: agents on a resource landscape generate wealth inequality, migration, trade, disease and conflict from local rules. It codified the "generative" standard of explanation ("if you didn't grow it, you didn't explain it") that underlies LLM-agent social simulation today.

strand: Emergence in social systems and agent-based models
citation: Axelrod, R. (1997). *The Dissemination of Culture: A Model with Local Convergence and Global Polarization*. Journal of Conflict Resolution, 41(2), 203–226. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022002797041002001
why: Agents with multi-feature cultures interact more with similar neighbors and become more similar, yet the population can freeze into distinct cultural regions. It is the canonical explanation of how homophily plus influence can preserve polarization, and a staple model in the physics of social dynamics.

strand: Emergence in social systems and agent-based models
citation: Macy, M. W., & Willer, R. (2002). *From Factors to Actors: Computational Sociology and Agent-Based Modeling*. Annual Review of Sociology, 28, 143–166. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.soc.28.110601.141117
why: The sociology-side manifesto for agent-based modeling: move from variable-centered regressions ("factors") to interacting adaptive agents ("actors"). It reviews emergent structure and emergent norms, and states the methodological principles (keep agents simple, test robustness) that reviewers still apply.

strand: Emergence in social systems and agent-based models
citation: Castellano, C., Fortunato, S., & Loreto, V. (2009). *Statistical physics of social dynamics*. Reviews of Modern Physics, 81(2), 591–646. https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.81.591
why: The definitive review of opinion, cultural, language and crowd dynamics as interacting-particle systems: order/disorder transitions, the role of network topology, voter, majority-rule, Sznajd, bounded-confidence and Axelrod models. It is the map of formal social-dynamics models and the most direct bridge from complexity to statistical mechanics and information theory.
focus: Sec. II General framework (A. Order and disorder: the Ising paradigm; B. Role of topology; C. Dynamical systems approach; D. Agent-based modeling); Sec. III Opinion dynamics (voter, majority rule, social impact, Sznajd, bounded confidence, empirical data); Sec. IV Cultural dynamics (Axelrod model); Sec. IX Social spreading phenomena; Sec. X Coevolution of states and topology

strand: Emergence in social systems and agent-based models
citation: Centola, D., & Macy, M. (2007). *Complex Contagions and the Weakness of Long Ties*. American Journal of Sociology, 113(3), 702–734. https://doi.org/10.1086/521848
why: Distinguishes simple contagions (one contact suffices, like disease or news) from complex contagions (several reinforcing contacts needed, like risky behavior or norms). For complex contagions, the long-range ties that make small worlds fast can slow diffusion, overturning a naive reading of Granovetter's "strength of weak ties."

citation: Watts, D. J., & Strogatz, S. H. (1998). *Collective dynamics of 'small-world' networks*. Nature, 393(6684), 440–442. https://doi.org/10.1038/30918
why: Shows that rewiring a few edges of a regular lattice gives short path lengths while keeping high clustering, and that this structure changes dynamics on the network. Listed as reference because the reader already knows network science; re-read it as a dynamics paper, not a topology paper.

citation: Barabási, A.-L., & Albert, R. (1999). *Emergence of Scaling in Random Networks*. Science, 286(5439), 509–512. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.286.5439.509
why: Growth plus preferential attachment generates a power-law degree distribution, giving a mechanistic story for "scale-free" networks. Read alongside Clauset et al. (2009) for the necessary statistical skepticism about claimed power laws.

citation: Barabási, A.-L. (with Pósfai, M.) (2016). *Network Science*. Cambridge University Press. Free interactive edition at networksciencebook.com.
why: A free, well-illustrated reference textbook for the network concepts that complex-systems arguments use. It is useful mainly for looking up specific results (robustness, spreading) rather than reading cover to cover, given the reader's background.
focus: Ch. 4 The Scale-Free Property; Ch. 5 The Barabási-Albert Model; Ch. 8 Network Robustness; Ch. 10 Spreading Phenomena

citation: Bak, P., Tang, C., & Wiesenfeld, K. (1987). *Self-organized criticality: An explanation of the 1/f noise*. Physical Review Letters, 59(4), 381–384. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.59.381
why: Introduces the sandpile model: a slowly driven system organizes itself, with no parameter tuning, into a critical state where avalanches of all sizes follow power laws. Self-organized criticality became the field's flagship explanation for heavy tails and bursty cascades (including attention and information cascades). Bak's popular book *How Nature Works* (1996) is the gentle companion.

citation: Scheffer, M., Bascompte, J., Brock, W. A., Brovkin, V., Carpenter, S. R., Dakos, V., Held, H., van Nes, E. H., Rietkerk, M., & Sugihara, G. (2009). *Early-warning signals for critical transitions*. Nature, 461(7260), 53–59. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature08227
why: Shows that systems approaching a fold bifurcation recover more slowly from small shocks ("critical slowing down"), which shows up as rising variance and autocorrelation in time series. It turns tipping points from metaphor into something measurable, with direct use for climate, ecosystems, markets and opinion shifts.

citation: Bettencourt, L. M. A., Lobo, J., Helbing, D., Kühnert, C., & West, G. B. (2007). *Growth, innovation, scaling, and the pace of life in cities*. PNAS, 104(17), 7301–7306. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0610172104
why: City-level quantities scale as power laws of population: infrastructure sublinearly (economies of scale), and wages, patents and crime superlinearly, so larger cities are "faster." It is the core empirical paper behind West's popular book *Scale* and a model of how scaling exponents reveal social-network mechanisms.

citation: Clauset, A., Shalizi, C. R., & Newman, M. E. J. (2009). *Power-Law Distributions in Empirical Data*. SIAM Review, 51(4), 661–703. https://doi.org/10.1137/070710111
why: The methodological corrective to the field's habit of seeing power laws everywhere: fit by maximum likelihood, choose x_min by minimizing the KS distance, test goodness-of-fit, and compare to lognormal and other alternatives with likelihood ratios. Many celebrated power laws fail the test, which is essential discipline for anyone measuring heavy-tailed social data.
focus: Sec. 3 Fitting power laws to empirical data; Sec. 4 Testing the power-law hypothesis; Sec. 5 Alternative distributions; Sec. 6 Applications to real-world data

citation: Sayama, H. (2015). *Introduction to the Modeling and Analysis of Complex Systems*. Open SUNY Textbooks. ISBN 9781942341093. CC BY-NC-SA.
why: A free, Python-based textbook that takes the reader from discrete and continuous dynamical systems through bifurcations, chaos, cellular automata, dynamical networks and agent-based models, with code throughout. It is the most efficient way for a daily Python user to turn the concepts in this canon into running models.
focus: Ch. 4–5 Discrete-Time Models I–II; Ch. 7 Continuous-Time Models II: Analysis; Ch. 8 Bifurcations; Ch. 9 Chaos; Ch. 11–12 Cellular Automata I–II; Ch. 16–18 Dynamical Networks I–III; Ch. 19 Agent-Based Models

citation: Thurner, S., Hanel, R., & Klimek, P. (2018). *Introduction to the Theory of Complex Systems*. Oxford University Press. ISBN 9780198821939.
why: The most mathematical general textbook, treating complex systems through probability, scaling, networks, evolutionary processes and, distinctively, generalized entropies and information theory for non-ergodic, path-dependent systems. It is the natural graduate-depth bridge to the foundational information-theory and probability readings.
focus: Ch. 1 Introduction to complex systems; Ch. 3 Scaling; Ch. 5 Evolutionary processes; Ch. 6 Statistical mechanics & information theory for complex systems

citation: Page, S. E. (2018). *The Model Thinker: What You Need to Know to Make Data Work for You*. Basic Books. ISBN 9780465094639.
why: A catalog of a few dozen core models (networks, diffusion, Markov processes, threshold and tipping models, game-theoretic models, and more) with the "many-model thinking" argument that combining models beats relying on any one. Useful as a lookup when deciding which model family fits a social phenomenon.
focus: whole (use as a reference, model by model)

citation: Mitchell, M. (instructor). *Introduction to Complexity*. Santa Fe Institute, Complexity Explorer (10 units, self-paced online course).
why: SFI's flagship free online course, effectively the video companion to Mitchell (2009), with NetLogo exercises. Its syllabus is a useful outside check on what the field considers introductory: what is complexity, dynamics and chaos, fractals, information, genetic algorithms, cellular automata, self-organization, cooperation, networks, and scaling.
focus: Units "What is Complexity?", "Dynamics and Chaos", "Information, Order, and Randomness", "Models of Cooperation in Social Systems", "Scaling in Biology and Society"

citation: Maxwell, J. C. (1868). *On Governors*. Proceedings of the Royal Society of London, 16, 270–283. https://doi.org/10.1098/rspl.1867.0055
why: The founding paper of control theory. Maxwell takes the steam-engine governor, a device that seemed to be pure engineering craft, linearizes its motion, and shows that whether it settles down or "hunts" (oscillates) depends on the roots of a polynomial. That move, stability as a property of characteristic roots, is still the core of the field.
focus: whole (14 pages; the opening classification of governors and the stability conditions are the essentials)

citation: Wiener, N. (1948). *Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine*. MIT Press (2nd ed. 1961; MIT Press reissue 2019, ISBN 9780262537841).
why: The book that named the field and claimed that control and communication are one subject across machines, animals and societies.
