Its central idea is that purposeful behavior is negative feedback driven by information about error. Much of it is heavy, dated mathematics, so read it for the framing and the history (anti-aircraft prediction, the nervous system, society) rather than for technique.
focus: whole, skimming the mathematics (read for the framing)
translation: 『サイバネティックス――動物と機械における制御と通信』池原止戈夫ほか訳, 岩波書店（岩波文庫）, 2011

citation: Ashby, W. R. (1956). *An Introduction to Cybernetics*. Chapman & Hall, London.
why: The clearest textbook of cybernetics ever written. It needs only high-school mathematics, yet it states the deepest principles: systems as transformations, the black box, variety (number of possible states), and the law of requisite variety, which says that only variety in the regulator can absorb variety in the disturbances. It is the conceptual root of the "good regulator" theorem and of much systems thinking in the social sciences.
focus: Ch. 4 The Machine with Input (incl. "Feedback"); Ch. 6 The Black Box; Ch. 7 Quantity of Variety; Ch. 10 Regulation in Biological Systems; Ch. 11 Requisite Variety; Ch. 12 The Error-Controlled Regulator
access: free: http://pespmc1.vub.ac.be/books/IntroCyb.pdf (electronic edition published by Principia Cybernetica with permission of the Ashby estate)
translation: 『サイバネティクス入門』篠崎武・山崎英三・銀林浩訳, 宇野書店, 1967

citation: Conant, R. C., & Ashby, W. R. (1970). *Every good regulator of a system must be a model of that system*. International Journal of Systems Science, 1(2), 89–97. https://doi.org/10.1080/00207727008920220
why: A short theorem with a famous title: the simplest optimal regulator of a system must contain (be isomorphic to) a model of that system. It is the formal ancestor of the idea that brains, organizations and AI agents must carry internal models of what they control. Read it alongside Ashby's Ch. 11, and be careful: the theorem is narrower than its title suggests.

citation: Meadows, D. H. (2008). *Thinking in Systems: A Primer* (D. Wright, Ed.). Chelsea Green Publishing, White River Junction, VT.
why: The best non-mathematical on-ramp: stocks, flows, balancing (negative) and reinforcing (positive) feedback loops, and delays, explained with everyday examples. It also gives the vocabulary that policy and sustainability researchers use (system traps, leverage points). Use it to build intuition before the equations, and as a check on whether you can explain a model in plain words.
focus: Ch. 1 The Basics; Ch. 2 A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo; Ch. 5 System Traps . . . and Opportunities; Ch. 6 Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
translation: 『世界はシステムで動く――いま起きていることの本質をつかむ考え方』枝廣淳子訳, 英治出版, 2015

citation: Åström, K. J., & Murray, R. M. (2021). *Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers* (2nd ed.). Princeton University Press. ISBN 9780691193984.
why: The standard modern introduction, written for scientists rather than only engineers, and the textbook of Caltech CDS 110. It covers why feedback works (disturbance rejection, robustness, tracking), state-space models, stability, reachability and observability, LQR, the Kalman filter, transfer functions, Bode/Nyquist, and PID, with examples from cruise control and bicycles to drug dosing and population dynamics. The figures are reproducible in Python with the `python-control` package.
focus: Ch. 1 Introduction; Ch. 2 Feedback Principles (incl. 2.6 Positive Feedback); Ch. 4 Examples (4.1 Cruise Control, 4.2 Bicycle Dynamics); Ch. 5 Dynamic Behavior (5.3 Stability); Ch. 7 State Feedback (7.1 Reachability, 7.5 Linear Quadratic Regulators); Ch. 8 Output Feedback (8.1 Observability, 8.4 Kalman Filtering); Ch. 11 PID Control

citation: Douglas, B. (n.d.). *Classical Control Theory* [YouTube playlist, "Control Systems Lectures"]. https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLUMWjy5jgHK1NC52DXXrriwihVrYZKqjk
why: Short (5–15 minute) whiteboard lectures by a practicing control engineer that build intuition for closed-loop control, transfer functions and Bode plots without heavy notation. They are a good audio-visual companion to Åström & Murray Ch. 1–2 and 9–11 for a learner starting from high-school math.
focus: "Why Learn Control Theory"; "Closed Loop Control"; "Transfer Functions"; "Bode Plots, Introduction"; "Final Value Theorem and Steady State Error"

citation: Kalman, R. E. (1960). *A New Approach to Linear Filtering and Prediction Problems*. Journal of Basic Engineering, 82(1), 35–45. https://doi.org/10.1115/1.3662552
why: Introduces the Kalman filter: a recursive algorithm that keeps a running best estimate of a hidden state and its uncertainty, predicting forward with a model and correcting with each new noisy measurement. It replaced Wiener's frequency-domain filtering with a state-space formulation that computers could run, and it went on to guide Apollo, GPS and almost every tracking system. Read it after Welch & Bishop.

citation: Kalman, R. E. (1960). *On the general theory of control systems*. IFAC Proceedings Volumes, 1(1), 491–502 (First IFAC World Congress, Moscow). https://doi.org/10.1016/S1474-6670(17)70094-8
why: The paper that introduced controllability and observability and showed their duality: whether inputs can steer every state, and whether outputs reveal every state, are mirror-image questions. These two concepts organize all of modern state-space control. Read the textbook treatments (Åström & Murray Ch. 7–8, Boyd's EE263 lectures) first; this is the historical source.

citation: Welch, G., & Bishop, G. (1995; updated 2004). *An Introduction to the Kalman Filter*. Technical Report TR 95-041, Department of Computer Science, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.
why: The most-used practical tutorial on the Kalman filter: 16 pages giving the predict–correct equations, the extended Kalman filter for nonlinear systems, and a worked example with real numbers. It is the fastest way to get the filter running in Python before reading Kalman or Särkkä.
focus: The Discrete Kalman Filter; A Kalman Filter in Action: Estimating a Random Constant

citation: Särkkä, S., & Svensson, L. (2023). *Bayesian Filtering and Smoothing* (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press. ISBN 9781108926645.
why: Rebuilds the Kalman filter from Bayes' rule: filtering is just recursive Bayesian updating of a belief about a hidden state, and the Kalman filter is the exact answer when everything is linear and Gaussian. From there it climbs to extended/unscented filters, particle filters and smoothers. This is the bridge between control and the Bayesian canon, and the natural tool for tracking latent opinion or attention over time.
focus: Ch. 1 What Are Bayesian Filtering and Smoothing?; Ch. 3 Batch and Recursive Bayesian Estimation; Ch. 6 Bayesian Filtering Equations and Exact Solutions; Ch. 7 Extended Kalman Filtering; Ch. 11 Particle Filtering; Ch. 12 Bayesian Smoothing Equations and Exact Solutions

citation: Boyd, S. (2007–08). *EE263: Introduction to Linear Dynamical Systems* [lecture notes, homework and videos]. Stanford Engineering Everywhere, Stanford University.
why: The classic applied course connecting linear algebra to dynamics: eigenvalues as modes of motion, the matrix exponential, inputs and outputs, controllability as a least-norm problem, and observability as a least-squares problem. It shows that state estimation and control are linear algebra with a time index. (Stanford has since split it into a new EE263 and EE363; this archived version is the classic.)
focus: Lectures "Autonomous linear dynamical systems"; "Eigenvectors and diagonalization"; "Linear dynamical systems with inputs and outputs"; "Controllability and state transfer"; "Observability and state estimation"

citation: Brunton, S. L. (2017–). *Control Bootcamp* [YouTube playlist]. University of Washington. https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLMrJAkhIeNNR20Mz-VpzgfQs5zrYi085m
why: A compact, code-along lecture series on modern state-space control: linear systems, stability and eigenvalues, controllability, pole placement, LQR, observability, and the Kalman filter, all worked on the inverted pendulum on a cart. It is the best single video path from "what is feedback" to "I can design an LQG controller", and it pairs naturally with Åström & Murray Ch. 5–8.
focus: "Control Bootcamp: Overview"; "Linear Systems"; "Stability and Eigenvalues"; "Controllability"; "Inverted Pendulum on a Cart"; "Kalman Filter Example in Matlab"; "Cruise Control Example with Proportional-Integral (PI) control"

citation: Bellman, R. (1957). *Dynamic Programming*. Princeton University Press (Dover reprint 2003, ISBN 9780486428093).
why: States the principle of optimality: an optimal plan has the property that, whatever the first decision, the remaining decisions must be optimal for the situation that results. This turns long-horizon decisions into a recursion on a "value function" (the Bellman equation), which underlies optimal control, economics' dynamic models, and all of reinforcement learning.
focus: Book TOC not verified here. Start with Bellman's free 4-page precursor, "On the Theory of Dynamic Programming", PNAS 38(8), 716–719 (1952), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1063639/ (doi:10.1073/pnas.38.8.716), then read the book's opening chapters.

citation: Liberzon, D. (2012). *Calculus of Variations and Optimal Control Theory: A Concise Introduction*. Princeton University Press. ISBN 9780691151878.
why: The cleanest path through the three classical routes to optimal control: calculus of variations, Pontryagin's maximum principle (optimality via "costates" or shadow prices), and the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation (optimality via a value function), ending with the linear-quadratic regulator. It replaces the hard-to-read original Pontryagin et al. (1962) and Kirk (1970) for a modern reader.
focus: Ch. 2 Calculus of Variations; Ch. 3 From Calculus of Variations to Optimal Control; Ch. 4 The Maximum Principle; Ch. 5 The Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation; Ch. 6 The Linear Quadratic Regulator

citation: Sutton, R. S., & Barto, A. G. (2018). *Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction* (2nd ed.). MIT Press. ISBN 9780262039246.
why: The defining textbook of reinforcement learning: an agent learns to act by trial and error from a reward signal, without a known model of its world. It frames RL as approximate dynamic programming (Markov decision processes, value functions, Bellman equations) and adds the learning ideas (temporal-difference learning, Q-learning, policy gradients). The psychology and neuroscience chapters connect RL to conditioning and dopamine.
focus: Ch. 1 Introduction (incl. 1.5 Tic-Tac-Toe, 1.7 Early History of Reinforcement Learning); Ch. 2 Multi-armed Bandits; Ch. 3 Finite Markov Decision Processes; Ch. 4 Dynamic Programming; Ch. 6 Temporal-Difference Learning; Ch. 13 Policy Gradient Methods; Ch. 14 Psychology; Ch. 15 Neuroscience
translation: 『強化学習（第2版）』今井翔太ほか訳, 森北出版, 2022

citation: Recht, B. (2019). *A Tour of Reinforcement Learning: The View from Continuous Control*. Annual Review of Control, Robotics, and Autonomous Systems, 2, 253–279. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-control-053018-023825
why: A control theorist's review of RL, written to give the control and RL communities a shared language. Its key move is to test RL methods on the simplest control problem with a known answer (LQR with unknown dynamics), and it finds that model-based approaches (estimate the model, then control) are often far more data-efficient than model-free ones. It is the best antidote to hype and the best bridge between strands 3 and 4.
focus: sections "What is reinforcement learning?"; "Strategies for solving reinforcement learning problems"; "Model-based reinforcement learning"; "Approximate Dynamic Programming"; "Direct Policy Search"

citation: Bertsekas, D. P. (2026). *A Course in Reinforcement Learning* (2nd ed.). Athena Scientific, Belmont, MA. ISBN 978-1-886529-29-8.
why: The optimal-control view of RL from the author of the standard dynamic-programming texts. It reads AlphaZero-style systems as approximation in value space plus online lookahead (rollout), and links RL to Newton's method and model predictive control. It is a free substitute for his paid *Reinforcement Learning and Optimal Control* (2019) and *Dynamic Programming and Optimal Control* (Vol. I, 4th ed., 2017).
focus: Ch. 1 Exact and Approximate Dynamic Programming (1.1 AlphaZero, Off-Line Training, and On-Line Play; 1.2 Deterministic Dynamic Programming; 1.5 Newton's Method - Linear Quadratic Problems; 1.7 Reinforcement Learning and Decision/Control); Ch. 2 Approximation in Value Space - Rollout Algorithms
access: free: https://www.mit.edu/~dimitrib/RLCOURSECOMPLETE%202ndEDITION.pdf (author's site, free for instructional use)

citation: Ng, A. Y., & Russell, S. (2000). *Algorithms for Inverse Reinforcement Learning*. Proceedings of the 17th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2000), 663–670.
why: Turns RL around: given an agent's (presumed optimal) behavior, infer the reward function it is optimizing. It also shows the problem is ill-posed (many rewards, including zero reward, explain any behavior) and proposes margin-based fixes. This is the computational core shared with Bayesian inverse planning in theory of mind and with preference learning in LLM alignment.

citation: Cannon, W. B. (1932). *The Wisdom of the Body*. W. W. Norton, New York.
why: Coins and popularizes "homeostasis": the body actively holds temperature, blood sugar, water and salt within narrow ranges through automatic corrective mechanisms. It is the biological template for every later "system that defends a set point". Its epilogue speculates on homeostasis in society, which anticipates cybernetic social science by fifteen years.
focus: Epilogue "Relations of Biological and Social Homeostasis" (pp. 305–324 of the 1932 edition) plus the opening chapters
translation: 『からだの知恵――この不思議なはたらき』舘鄰・舘澄江訳, 講談社学術文庫, 1981

citation: Powers, W. T. (1973). *Behavior: The Control of Perception*. Aldine, Chicago. (Revised text with added chapter "Emotion", 2005.)
why: Perceptual Control Theory: organisms do not control their actions, they act in order to keep their *perceptions* at reference values, and behavior is organized as a hierarchy of such control loops. The thesis reverses the stimulus–response picture and gives a concrete control-theoretic model of purpose. It is outside the mainstream, but it is a sharp lens for agent-based models of goal-directed actors.
focus: Chapters "Feedback and Behavior"; "The Control-System Unit of Organization"; "A Hierarchy of Control Systems"; "Conflict and Control" (titles as in the revised text)

citation: Todorov, E., & Jordan, M. I. (2002). *Optimal feedback control as a theory of motor coordination*. Nature Neuroscience, 5(11), 1226–1235. https://doi.org/10.1038/nn963
why: Shows that the brain's movement control looks like stochastic optimal feedback control (LQG-style estimation plus control), not like replaying a fixed planned trajectory. Its "minimal intervention principle" says that a good controller corrects only the deviations that hurt the task and lets harmless variability be. This is the landmark case of optimal control as a theory of cognition.
focus: whole (the minimal intervention principle section is the payoff)

citation: Wlezien, C. (1995). *The Public as Thermostat: Dynamics of Preferences for Spending*. American Journal of Political Science, 39(4), 981 ff. https://doi.org/10.2307/2111666
why: Models public opinion as a thermostat: the public's *relative* preference ("spend more" vs "spend less") falls when policy moves up and rises when it moves down, so opinion acts as negative feedback on policy. This made feedback a measurable, time-series idea in political science, and was extended in Soroka & Wlezien's *Degrees of Democracy* (Cambridge UP, 2010) into a theory of how media and institutions shape responsiveness. It is a direct template for studying opinion dynamics around crisis and climate policy.

citation: Beniger, J. R. (1986). *The Control Revolution: Technological and Economic Origins of the Information Society*. Harvard University Press, Cambridge, MA.
why: A communication scholar's grand history: the "information society" arose because industrialization sped up material flows faster than anyone could steer them, and a "crisis of control" was answered by bureaucracy, telecommunications, mass media and computing. It reframes media and information technology as control technology, which is the most direct link from cybernetics to communication research.

citation: Kydland, F. E., & Prescott, E. C. (1977). *Rules Rather than Discretion: The Inconsistency of Optimal Plans*. Journal of Political Economy, 85(3), 473–491. https://doi.org/10.1086/260580
why: Argues that optimal control theory "is not the appropriate tool" for economic policy when people form expectations about future policy: a plan that is optimal today becomes tempting to abandon tomorrow (time inconsistency), so binding rules can beat case-by-case optimization. It marks the limit of control theory when the "plant" is a population of strategic agents, and it was cited in the 2004 Nobel prize.
focus: whole (the introduction and the patent and flood-plain examples are the essentials)

citation: Taylor, J. B. (1993). *Discretion versus policy rules in practice*. Carnegie-Rochester Conference Series on Public Policy, 39, 195–214. https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-2231(93)90009-L
why: Proposes the Taylor rule: set the short-term interest rate as a simple linear function of inflation's gap from target and output's gap from potential. In control terms, it is a feedback law for the economy, and it became the benchmark central banks are judged against. Read it as the practical answer to Kydland & Prescott: a simple, transparent rule rather than discretion.

citation: von Neumann, J., & Morgenstern, O. (1944). *Theory of Games and Economic Behavior*. Princeton University Press. 60th Anniversary Commemorative Edition (2004/2007), with an introduction by H. W. Kuhn and an afterword by A. Rubinstein, 776 pp.
why: This is the founding text of game theory. It proposed treating economic interaction as a "game of strategy" and proved the zero-sum minimax machinery. Its utility appendix gave the axioms behind von Neumann–Morgenstern (cardinal) expected utility. Read it for its framing and its axioms, not as a textbook.
focus: Ch. I "Formulation of the Economic Problem"; Appendix "The Axiomatic Treatment of Utility"; skim Ch. III "Zero-Sum Two-Person Games: Theory".
translation: JA: 『ゲームの理論と経済行動』 (銀林浩ほか訳, 東京図書); ZH: 《博弈论与经济行为》 (王文玉、王宇译, 生活·读书·新知三联书店)

citation: Savage, L. J. (1954). *The Foundations of Statistics*. Wiley. 2nd rev. ed., Dover Publications, 1972, 310 pp.
why: Savage derives subjective probability and expected utility together from postulates about preferences over acts. One of them is the "sure-thing principle" that Allais and Ellsberg later attacked. This is the standard axiomatic basis for Bayesian decision theory, and the book every later decision paradox is measured against.
focus: whole (chapter-level table of contents not verified; the opening chapters, which build the postulates, are the essential part)

citation: Allais, M. (1953). Le Comportement de l'Homme Rationnel devant le Risque: Critique des Postulats et Axiomes de l'Ecole Americaine. *Econometrica*, 21(4), 503 ff. DOI: 10.2307/1907921
why: This paper gives the original "common consequence" choice problems. Most people's answers violate the independence axiom of expected utility. The Allais paradox is the founding anomaly behind non-expected-utility theories, including prospect theory's probability weighting. The paper is in French; most readers meet the paradox through textbook restatements.
focus: the choice examples that state the paradox
verified: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.2307/1907921 (start page verified; end page not confirmed)

citation: Ellsberg, D. (1961). Risk, Ambiguity, and the Savage Axioms. *The Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 75(4), 643–669. DOI: 10.2307/1884324
why: Ellsberg used urn thought-experiments to show that people prefer known odds to unknown odds. This "ambiguity aversion" cannot be squared with any single subjective probability, so it breaks Savage's framework. It separates *risk* (known probabilities) from *ambiguity* (unknown probabilities), which matters for how publics react to uncertain science communication.

citation: Simon, H. A. (1955). A Behavioral Model of Rational Choice. *The Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 69(1), 99–118. DOI: 10.2307/1884852
why: Simon replaced the omniscient maximizer with an agent who has limited computation and information. That agent searches until an option meets an aspiration level ("satisficing"). Bounded rationality starts here, and both the heuristics-and-biases school and the ecological-rationality school claim this paper.

citation: Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases. *Science*, 185(4157), 1124–1131. DOI: 10.1126/science.185.4157.1124
why: This paper names three judgment heuristics: representativeness, availability, and anchoring-and-adjustment. It shows the systematic biases each one produces. It is the manifesto of the heuristics-and-biases program and the vocabulary behind most work on misinformation susceptibility.

citation: Kahneman, D., & Tversky, A. (1979). Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk. *Econometrica*, 47(2), 263–291. DOI: 10.2307/1914185
why: Prospect theory is the leading descriptive alternative to expected utility. People value gains and losses relative to a reference point, with losses looming larger (loss aversion). They also weight probabilities non-linearly. This is one of the most-cited papers in economics, and the MIT 14.13 syllabus assigns it as required reading.
focus: whole; the empirical "effects" sections first, then the value and weighting functions

citation: Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1981). The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice. *Science*, 211(4481), 453–458. DOI: 10.1126/science.7455683
why: This paper introduces the "Asian disease" problem. Logically equivalent descriptions ("200 saved" versus "400 die") reverse people's preferences, which violates description invariance. It is the bridge between decision theory and framing research in communication.

citation: Gigerenzer, G., & Brighton, H. (2009). Homo Heuristicus: Why Biased Minds Make Better Inferences. *Topics in Cognitive Science*, 1(1), 107–143. DOI: 10.1111/j.1756-8765.2008.01006.x
why: This is the counterweight to heuristics-and-biases. Simple heuristics can out-predict complex models when matched to the structure of the environment ("ecological rationality", "less-is-more"). The authors argue this through the bias–variance dilemma familiar from machine learning. It reframes "bias" as a possible adaptive trade-off rather than an error.

citation: Kahneman, D. (2011). *Thinking, Fast and Slow*. Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1st ed., 499 pp.
why: Kahneman's own popular synthesis of the heuristics-and-biases and prospect-theory programs, built around the System 1/System 2 metaphor. Use it as the on-ramp before the 1974, 1979 and 1981 papers. Read the priming material in Part I critically, because several studies cited there have since failed to replicate.
focus: Part II "Heuristics and Biases"; Part IV "Choices" (includes "Bernoulli's Errors", "Prospect Theory", "The Fourfold Pattern", "Frames and Reality"); Part I "Two Systems" for the framing metaphor.
translation: JA: 『ファスト＆スロー：あなたの意思はどのように決まるか？』

citation: Nash, J. F. (1950). Equilibrium Points in n-Person Games. *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, 36(1), 48–49. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.36.1.48
why: In two pages, Nash defines the equilibrium point (each player best-responds to the others) and proves via Kakutani's fixed-point theorem that every finite game has one in mixed strategies. Almost everything in non-cooperative game theory rests on this. The fuller version is Nash (1951), "Non-Cooperative Games", *Annals of Mathematics* 54(2), 286–295.

citation: Harsanyi, J. C. (1967–68). Games with Incomplete Information Played by "Bayesian" Players, I–III. *Management Science*: Part I "The Basic Model", 14(3), 159–182; Part II "Bayesian Equilibrium Points", 14(5), 320–334; Part III "The Basic Probability Distribution of the Game", 14(7), 486–502. DOI (Part I): 10.1287/mnsc.14.3.159
why: Harsanyi turned uncertainty about other players' payoffs into "types" drawn by Nature from a common prior. This made incomplete-information games analysable as Bayesian games, the basis of signaling, auctions and mechanism design. It is the formal home of "beliefs about beliefs".
focus: Part I first; Part II for Bayesian equilibrium

citation: Osborne, M. J. (2004). *An Introduction to Game Theory*. Oxford University Press.
why: The clearest rigorous undergraduate text. It builds each concept from many worked examples (Prisoner's Dilemma, BoS, Stag Hunt, Hawk–Dove, public goods). It assumes only basic maths, so it is the right primary textbook to work through with exercises.
focus: Ch. 1 Introduction; Ch. 2 Nash Equilibrium: Theory; Ch. 3 Nash Equilibrium: Illustrations; Ch. 4 Mixed Strategy Equilibrium; Ch. 5 Extensive Games with Perfect Information: Theory; Ch. 9 Bayesian Games; Ch. 13 Evolutionary Equilibrium; Ch. 14 Repeated Games: The Prisoner's Dilemma.
access: need-copy (penultimate-draft chapters 1–3 are free on the author's site: https://www.economics.utoronto.ca/osborne/igt/nash.pdf and https://www.economics.utoronto.ca/osborne/igt/INDEXR.HTM)

citation: Osborne, M. J., & Rubinstein, A. (1994). *A Course in Game Theory*. MIT Press, 352 pp.
why: A compact, rigorous graduate text, unusually careful about what solution concepts *mean*. It has a whole chapter on knowledge and equilibrium. The authors distribute it free, so it serves as the graduate reference in place of Fudenberg & Tirole.
focus: Ch. 2 Nash Equilibrium; Ch. 3 Mixed, Correlated, and Evolutionary Equilibrium; Ch. 4 Rationalizability and Iterated Elimination of Dominated Actions; Ch. 5 Knowledge and Equilibrium; Ch. 8 Repeated Games; Ch. 10 Implementation Theory.
access: free: https://books.osborne.economics.utoronto.ca/ (free PDF after registration with the authors)
translation: ZH: 《博弈论教程》 (魏玉根译, 中国社会科学出版社)

citation: Dixit, A. K., & Nalebuff, B. J. (2008). *The Art of Strategy: A Game Theorist's Guide to Success in Business and Life*. W. W. Norton, 512 pp. (Successor to their *Thinking Strategically*, Norton, 1991, which the Yale ECON 159 syllabus lists.)
why: The best non-technical on-ramp, written by two leading theorists. It teaches backward induction, commitment, credible threats, mixed strategies and brinkmanship through stories, giving strategic intuition before the formal apparatus.
translation: JA: 『戦略的思考をどう実践するか：エール大学式「ゲーム理論」の活用法』 (嶋津祐一・池村千秋訳, 阪急コミュニケーションズ)

citation: Polak, B. (2007). *ECON 159: Game Theory* (24 video lectures, Fall 2007). Open Yale Courses, Yale University.
why: A widely used free lecture course that builds the theory from applied examples (soccer, dating, voting, bank runs, auctions). It covers dominance, Nash equilibrium, mixed strategies, evolutionary stability, backward induction, subgame perfection, repeated games and asymmetric information. Pair it with Osborne for exercises.
focus: L1 "Introduction: Five First Lessons"; L2 "Putting Yourselves into Other People's Shoes"; L5–6 Nash equilibrium; L9 "Mixed Strategies in Theory and Tennis"; L11–12 Evolutionary Stability; L17 "Backward Induction: Ultimatums and Bargaining"; L21–22 Repeated Games; L23 "Asymmetric Information: Silence, Signaling and Suffering Education".

citation: Schelling, T. C. (1960). *The Strategy of Conflict*. Harvard University Press. (Paperback reissue with a new preface by the author, Harvard University Press, 1981, 328 pp.)
why: Schelling's "reorientation of game theory" toward mixed-motive bargaining. It introduces focal points (tacit coordination on salient solutions), commitment, and "the threat that leaves something to chance". Game theory meets communication here: what is *said* and what is *salient* changes equilibria.
focus: Part I "Elements of a Theory of Strategy" (esp. "An Essay on Bargaining"; "Bargaining, Communication, and Limited War"); Part II "A Reorientation of Game Theory" (esp. "Toward a Theory of Interdependent Decision"); Part III "The Threat That Leaves Something to Chance".
translation: JA: 『紛争の戦略：ゲーム理論のエッセンス』 (河野勝監訳, 勁草書房); ZH: 《冲突的战略》 (赵华等译, 华夏出版社)

citation: Aumann, R. J. (1976). Agreeing to Disagree. *The Annals of Statistics*, 4(6), 1236–1239. DOI: 10.1214/aos/1176343654
why: In four pages, Aumann gives the first formal definition of common knowledge (via information partitions). It proves that Bayesians with a common prior cannot have commonly known posteriors that differ. This is the formal anchor for every later discussion of persistent disagreement and polarization among "rational" agents.

citation: Rubinstein, A. (1989). The Electronic Mail Game: Strategic Behavior under "Almost Common Knowledge." *American Economic Review*, 79(3), 385–391.
why: Players coordinate through a chain of confirmation messages, and any message can be lost. No finite number of confirmations ever produces common knowledge, and coordination can unravel completely. It shows that "almost common knowledge" behaves very differently from common knowledge, a sharp result for any theory of communication and coordination.

citation: Geanakoplos, J. (1992). Common Knowledge. *Journal of Economic Perspectives*, 6(4), 53–82. DOI: 10.1257/jep.6.4.53
why: The best expository survey. It starts from puzzles (the hats, envelopes and detectives puzzles), builds the partition model of knowledge, and then derives agreeing-to-disagree, no-speculation results and the coordinated-attack problem studied by Rubinstein. Read this before Aumann and Rubinstein.
focus: whole; sections "Puzzles About Reasoning Based on the Reasoning of Others", "Interactive Epistemology", "Characterizing Common Knowledge of Events and Actions", "Speculation", "Infinite State Spaces and Knowledge about Knowledge to Level N"

citation: Nagel, R. (1995). Unraveling in Guessing Games: An Experimental Study. *American Economic Review*, 85(5), 1313–1326.
why: This is the first systematic experiment on the "guess p times the average" game, Keynes's beauty contest made precise. Choices cluster at one or two steps of iterated reasoning rather than at the Nash equilibrium of zero. It is the empirical seed of level-k and cognitive-hierarchy models.

citation: Camerer, C. F., Ho, T.-H., & Chong, J.-K. (2004). A Cognitive Hierarchy Model of Games. *The Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 119(3), 861–898. DOI: 10.1162/0033553041502225
why: This paper formalizes bounded strategic depth. Level-k players best-respond to a (Poisson) mix of lower-level players, and a single parameter (average thinking steps) fits many games better than Nash equilibrium. It is a ready-made template for modeling or benchmarking LLM agents' depth of strategic reasoning.

citation: McKelvey, R. D., & Palfrey, T. R. (1995). Quantal Response Equilibria for Normal Form Games. *Games and Economic Behavior*, 10(1), 6–38. DOI: 10.1006/game.1995.1023
why: QRE replaces exact best responses with noisy, probabilistic ones (typically a logit rule with a precision parameter λ), each consistent with the others' noisy play. It recovers Nash as λ→∞ and fits experimental deviations, and it is the standard stochastic-choice equilibrium for structural estimation.
focus: whole; the logit QRE definition first

citation: Camerer, C. F. (2003). *Behavioral Game Theory: Experiments in Strategic Interaction*. Princeton University Press / Russell Sage Foundation (Roundtable Series in Behavioral Economics), 544 pp.
why: The standard synthesis of experimental game theory. It covers what people actually do in ultimatum, dictator, trust, coordination, bargaining and dominance-solvable games, and which models (social preferences, learning, limited thinking) explain it. Use it as the evidence base against which textbook equilibria are checked.
translation: ZH: 《行为博弈：对策略互动的实验研究》 (贺京同等译, 中国人民大学出版社)

citation: Axelrod, R. (1984). *The Evolution of Cooperation*. Basic Books. (Revised ed., Basic Books, 2006, 241 pp.)
why: Axelrod ran computer tournaments of the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma, which TIT FOR TAT won. He drew lessons about when cooperation emerges without a central authority: be nice, retaliatory, forgiving and clear, and keep "the shadow of the future" long. This is the classic computational-social-science demonstration of cooperation through repeated interaction. (Core paper: Axelrod & Hamilton 1981, *Science* 211(4489), 1390–1396.)
translation: JA: 『つきあい方の科学：バクテリアから国際関係まで』 (松田裕之訳, ミネルヴァ書房); ZH: 《合作的进化》 (吴坚忠译, 上海人民出版社)

citation: Maynard Smith, J., & Price, G. R. (1973). The Logic of Animal Conflict. *Nature*, 246(5427), 15–18. DOI: 10.1038/246015a0
why: This paper introduces the evolutionarily stable strategy (ESS): a strategy that, once common, cannot be invaded by rare mutants. The authors use it to explain why animal contests are often "limited wars". It founded evolutionary game theory, where equilibrium comes from selection rather than rationality.

citation: Nowak, M. A. (2006). Five Rules for the Evolution of Cooperation. *Science*, 314(5805), 1560–1563. DOI: 10.1126/science.1133755
why: A compact unifying map of five mechanisms that sustain cooperation: kin selection, direct reciprocity, indirect reciprocity (reputation), network reciprocity, and group selection. Each comes with a simple benefit-to-cost threshold. Network reciprocity links directly to network science.

citation: Myerson, R. B. (2008). Perspectives on Mechanism Design in Economic Theory. *American Economic Review*, 98(3), 586–603. DOI: 10.1257/aer.98.3.586 (Nobel Prize Lecture, 8 December 2007)
why: One of the 2007 laureates explains "reverse game theory": designing the rules so that self-interested agents with private information produce a desired outcome. The lecture covers incentive compatibility and the revelation principle. It is the most readable entry from the Hurwicz/Maskin/Myerson prize. Companion: Maskin (2008), *AER* 98(3), 567–576, and the Prize Committee's scientific background "Mechanism Design Theory" (2007).

citation: The CORE Team (2023–, continuously updated). *The Economy 2.0: Microeconomics* and *The Economy 2.0: Macroeconomics*. CORE Econ, free online textbook (The Economy 1.0 still available).
why: This is the modern free introductory text. It is built around strategic interaction, incomplete contracts, inequality and crises rather than frictionless supply and demand, so information and power show up from the first units. It is the best single on-ramp for someone who wants the current mainstream picture without the 1980s textbook baggage.
focus: Micro: Unit 4 "Strategic interactions and social dilemmas", Unit 9 "Lenders and borrowers and differences in wealth", Unit 10 "Market successes and failures". Macro: Unit 6 "The financial sector: Debt, money, and financial markets", Unit 8 "Economic dynamics: Financial and environmental crises".

citation: Varian, H. R. (2014). *Intermediate Microeconomics: A Modern Approach* (9th ed.). W. W. Norton. ISBN 9780393123968.
why: This is the standard intermediate micro reference, and its notation is the one most papers in this list assume. Use it to look up consumer choice, uncertainty, asset markets, game theory, and asymmetric information as needed, not to read cover to cover.
focus: Use as a reference when a paper assumes a concept (chapters on uncertainty, asset markets, game theory, asymmetric information; chapter numbers not verified here).

citation: Heilbroner, R. L. (1999). *The Worldly Philosophers: The Lives, Times, and Ideas of the Great Economic Thinkers* (7th ed.). Touchstone / Simon & Schuster. ISBN 9780684862149.
why: It is the classic narrative history of economic thought, from Smith through Marx, Veblen, Keynes and Schumpeter. It gives the intellectual genealogy behind the debates in this canon, for example why Keynes's emphasis on uncertainty mattered so much, and it is very readable.

citation: Hayek, F. A. (1945). The Use of Knowledge in Society. *American Economic Review*, 35(4), 519–530.
why: It recasts the economic problem as using knowledge that is dispersed, local and tacit, rather than as optimizing given known data. The price system is presented as a mechanism that compresses and transmits that knowledge, and Hayek himself compares it to "a system of telecommunications". It is the founding text for treating markets as information processors.

citation: Akerlof, G. A. (1970). The Market for "Lemons": Quality Uncertainty and the Market Mechanism. *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 84(3), 488–500. https://doi.org/10.2307/1879431
why: It shows that when sellers know quality and buyers do not, average-quality pricing drives good products out, and a market can unravel completely. This adverse-selection logic now explains insurance, credit, labor markets, and arguably markets for information and content too.

citation: Spence, M. (1973). Job Market Signaling. *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 87(3), 355–374. https://doi.org/10.2307/1882010
why: It is the counterpart to Akerlof: the informed side takes a costly action, such as education, to reveal its type, and the outcome is a separating equilibrium in which beliefs and actions confirm each other. It is the prototype signaling game, and costly signaling reappears in biology, credentials and online reputation.
focus: whole. A free companion is Spence's 2001 Nobel lecture "Signaling in Retrospect and the Informational Structure of Markets": https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2018/06/spence-lecture.pdf

citation: Fama, E. F. (1970). Efficient Capital Markets: A Review of Theory and Empirical Work. *Journal of Finance*, 25(2), 383–417. https://doi.org/10.2307/2325486
why: It defines market efficiency as prices "fully reflecting" available information and introduces the weak, semi-strong and strong forms. It also makes the joint-hypothesis problem explicit: efficiency can only be tested together with a model of expected returns. Every later debate about bubbles, anomalies and behavioral finance argues with this paper.
focus: whole. A free companion is Fama's 2013 Nobel lecture "Two Pillars of Asset Pricing": https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2018/06/fama-lecture.pdf

citation: Grossman, S. J., & Stiglitz, J. E. (1980). On the Impossibility of Informationally Efficient Markets. *American Economic Review*, 70(3), 393–408.
why: If prices fully revealed information, nobody would pay to gather it, so prices cannot be fully informative. Equilibrium therefore needs noise, and an "equilibrium degree of disequilibrium". The noisy rational-expectations model in this paper is the cleanest place to see price as a noisy Bayesian signal.

citation: Stiglitz, J. E. (2002). Information and the Change in the Paradigm in Economics. *American Economic Review*, 92(3), 460–501. https://doi.org/10.1257/00028280260136363 (Nobel Prize lecture delivered 8 December 2001.)
why: It is a long, accessible survey of the whole information-economics program: screening, signaling, efficiency wages, credit rationing, and the failure of the invisible-hand theorems under imperfect information. It works as a map that connects Akerlof, Spence, Grossman–Stiglitz and much of macro-finance.
focus: whole (the Nobel PDF is the free version)

citation: Keynes, J. M. (1936). *The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money*. Macmillan. Chapter 12, "The State of Long-Term Expectation".
why: Chapter 12 is where Keynes argues that long-term expectations rest on fragile convention rather than calculable probability. It contains the "beauty contest" image of investors guessing what average opinion expects average opinion to be, and the "animal spirits" that drive investment. It is the origin of higher-order-belief thinking in economics.
access: free: https://gutenberg.net.au/ebooks03/0300071h/printall.html (public domain in Australia and in Japan, since Keynes died in 1946; still under copyright in the US until 2032, so check local law)

citation: Muth, J. F. (1961). Rational Expectations and the Theory of Price Movements. *Econometrica*, 29(3), 315–335. https://doi.org/10.2307/1909635
why: It proposes that agents' subjective expectations equal the model's own predictions, so expectations are endogenous and model-consistent rather than ad hoc. This became the default assumption of modern macro and finance, and it is the baseline that behavioral and narrative economics depart from.

citation: Lucas, R. E., Jr. (1976). Econometric Policy Evaluation: A Critique. *Carnegie-Rochester Conference Series on Public Policy*, 1, 19–46. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0167-2231(76)80003-6
why: Estimated behavioral relationships embed agents' expectations about policy, so they shift when policy changes. Models fitted to past data therefore mislead about interventions. This is the economist's version of the distinction between a structural (invariant) model and a reduced-form correlation.
focus: whole. A free companion is Lucas's 1995 Nobel lecture "Monetary Neutrality": https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2018/06/lucas-lecture.pdf

citation: Morris, S., & Shin, H. S. (2002). Social Value of Public Information. *American Economic Review*, 92(5), 1521–1534. https://doi.org/10.1257/000282802762024610
why: It formalizes Keynes's beauty contest. When agents also want to match each other's actions, they over-weight public signals because those signals predict what others believe. As a result, more precise public information, such as central-bank communication, can lower welfare. It is the key model for how broadcast information shapes coordination, with direct relevance to media and misinformation research.

citation: Shiller, R. J. (2019). *Narrative Economics: How Stories Go Viral and Drive Major Economic Events*. Princeton University Press. ISBN 9780691182292.
why: Shiller argues that contagious popular stories drive economic fluctuations and models their spread with epidemic (SIR-type) dynamics. Examples include the Laffer curve, Bitcoin, and stories of technological unemployment. It is the most direct bridge from economics to communication research and computational text analysis, and it matches Kunhao's narrative-economics data interests.
focus: whole. A free precursor is Shiller's 2017 AEA presidential address, *AER* 107(4), 967–1004 (NBER WP 23075).

citation: Shiller, R. J. (2015). *Irrational Exuberance* (revised and expanded 3rd ed.). Princeton University Press. https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400865536
why: It is the empirical case that stock, bond and housing prices undergo speculative bubbles amplified by feedback loops, news media and "new era" stories. It is the data-driven companion to *Narrative Economics*. Shiller's 2013 Nobel lecture "Speculative Asset Prices" summarizes the research: https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2018/06/shiller-lecture.pdf
focus: whole (the chapters on cultural and psychological factors and on news media are most relevant; chapter numbers not verified here)

citation: Thaler, R. H. (2015). *Misbehaving: The Making of Behavioral Economics*. W. W. Norton. ISBN 9780393080940.
why: It is a first-person history of how anomalies such as mental accounting, the endowment effect, self-control problems and limits to arbitrage pushed economics to admit "Humans" alongside "Econs". It is the most readable on-ramp to behavioral economics and behavioral finance. Thaler & Sunstein's *Nudge* and Kahneman & Tversky (1979) are cross-referenced to the decision-theory canon.

citation: Markowitz, H. (1952). Portfolio Selection. *Journal of Finance*, 7(1), 77–91. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1952.tb01525.x
why: It turns investing into a trade-off between mean and variance. Diversification falls out of the covariance matrix, and the efficient frontier is born. This is the linear-algebra core of all modern portfolio theory, CAPM and factor models.
focus: whole. A free companion is Markowitz's 1990 Nobel lecture "Foundations of Portfolio Theory": https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2018/06/markowitz-lecture.pdf

citation: Black, F., & Scholes, M. (1973). The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities. *Journal of Political Economy*, 81(3), 637–654. https://doi.org/10.1086/260062
why: It prices an option by building a riskless hedge, so the price depends on volatility but not on anyone's beliefs about expected return. That is a striking case of beliefs dropping out of prices. The pricing equation is a diffusion (heat-type) PDE, and the paper founded derivatives markets.

citation: Kelly, J. L., Jr. (1956). A New Interpretation of Information Rate. *Bell System Technical Journal*, 35(4), 917–926. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1956.tb03809.x
why: A gambler with a private noisy channel who bets to maximize long-run wealth growth achieves a growth rate equal to Shannon's information rate of the channel. It is the literal bridge between information theory and investing, later popularized by Thorp, and it underlies "log-optimal" portfolio theory. This entry is cross-referenced to the information-theory canon.

citation: Lo, A. W. (2017). *Adaptive Markets: Financial Evolution at the Speed of Thought*. Princeton University Press. ISBN 9780691135144.
why: It reconciles efficient markets with behavioral finance through evolution. Market efficiency depends on the current population of strategies and the environment, so it waxes and wanes, and heuristics are adaptations rather than errors. It gives an ecological and complex-systems reading of finance.

citation: Mandelbrot, B., & Hudson, R. L. (2004). *The (Mis)Behavior of Markets: A Fractal View of Risk, Ruin, and Reward*. Basic Books. ISBN 9780465043552.
why: It is a popular but serious critique of Gaussian finance. Price changes are fat-tailed, volatility clusters, and dependence is long-memory, so standard risk models badly underprice crashes. It is the conceptual entry point to power laws and scaling in markets.

citation: Bodie, Z., Kane, A., & Marcus, A. J. (2023). *Investments*. McGraw-Hill Education. ISBN 9781264412662 (current edition; the 2020 edition is ISBN 9781260013832).
why: It is the standard MBA and upper-UG investments text: portfolio theory, CAPM and factor models, efficient markets and behavioral finance, fixed income and derivatives. Use it to look up mechanics and formulas when reading the papers.
focus: Use as a reference (chapter numbers not verified here).

citation: Diamond, D. W., & Dybvig, P. H. (1983). Bank Runs, Deposit Insurance, and Liquidity. *Journal of Political Economy*, 91(3), 401–419. https://doi.org/10.1086/261155 (Reprinted in Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis *Quarterly Review*, 24(1), Winter 2000.)
why: Banks transform illiquid assets into liquid deposits, which creates two equilibria: a good one and a self-fulfilling run in which each depositor withdraws because they expect others to. It is the canonical model of a crisis driven purely by beliefs, and it explains why deposit insurance works. It contributed to the 2022 Nobel prize.

citation: Minsky, H. P. (1992). The Financial Instability Hypothesis. Working Paper No. 74, Jerome Levy Economics Institute of Bard College. (Prepared for P. Arestis & M. Sawyer (Eds.), *Handbook of Radical Political Economy*, Edward Elgar, 1993.)
why: In about 10 pages, Minsky argues that stability breeds instability. Calm periods push financing from hedge to speculative to "Ponzi" positions, until a reversal forces debt deflation. It is the standard reference for the "Minsky moment" and complements the equilibrium-based Diamond–Dybvig model.

citation: Aliber, R. Z., & Kindleberger, C. P. (2015). *Manias, Panics, and Crashes: A History of Financial Crises* (7th ed.). Palgrave Macmillan. ISBN 9781137525758.
why: Kindleberger's classic, updated by Aliber, uses a Minsky-style anatomy (displacement, boom, euphoria, distress, revulsion) to read four centuries of bubbles and panics, along with the role of the lender of last resort. It is the historian's complement to the formal models.

citation: Reinhart, C. M., & Rogoff, K. S. (2009). *This Time Is Different: Eight Centuries of Financial Folly*. Princeton University Press. https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400831722
why: It compiles a quantitative database of sovereign defaults, banking crises, inflations and currency crashes across eight centuries. Its main finding is that crises recur with striking regularity, while each generation's belief that "this time is different" recurs too. Use it as an empirical reference rather than reading it straight through.

citation: Koo, R. C. (2009). *The Holy Grail of Macroeconomics: Lessons from Japan's Great Recession* (rev. ed.). John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 9780470824948 (1st ed. 2008, ISBN 9780470823873).
why: After the 1990 asset-price collapse, Japanese firms switched from maximizing profit to minimizing debt. This "balance-sheet recession" made monetary policy ineffective and required fiscal support. Koo is a Nomura economist, so the book is an influential practitioner view written from inside Japan, and it was widely re-read after 2008.

citation: Hoshi, T., & Kashyap, A. K. (2004). Japan's Financial Crisis and Economic Stagnation. *Journal of Economic Perspectives*, 18(1), 3–26. https://doi.org/10.1257/089533004773563412
why: It is a concise, credible academic account of Japan's lost decade. Banks hid bad loans and kept lending to insolvent "zombie" firms, and the authors analyze the regulatory forbearance that let this happen. It counterweights Koo's demand-side story with a banking and incentives story.

citation: Arthur, W. B. (1994). Inductive Reasoning and Bounded Rationality. *American Economic Review*, 84(2), 406–411.
why: In the El Farol bar problem, agents decide whether to attend a bar that is fun only if it is not crowded. Any commonly shared forecast defeats itself, so agents must use an evolving ecology of inductive hypotheses, and attendance self-organizes around capacity. It is the founding agent-based model of self-referential expectations and leads directly to the minority game and social simulation.

citation: Farmer, J. D. (2024). *Making Sense of Chaos: A Better Economics for a Better World*. Yale University Press. ISBN 9780300273779.
why: A Santa Fe and Oxford physicist-economist makes the case for complexity economics: heterogeneous boundedly rational agents, agent-based simulation, out-of-equilibrium dynamics and data-driven models, applied to crashes, climate and policy. It is the up-to-date manifesto for the simulation-heavy approach closest to Kunhao's methods. It is cross-referenced to the complex-systems canon.

citation: Shannon, C. E. (1948). *A Mathematical Theory of Communication*. Bell System Technical Journal, 27(3), 379–423 and 27(4), 623–656. DOI 10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb01338.x (Part 1); 10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb00917.x (Part 2).
why: This is the founding document. It defines information as reduction of uncertainty (entropy), separates the source from the channel, and proves that error-free communication is possible at any rate below capacity. Its "approximations to English" (random text generated from letter and word statistics) are an ancestor of n-gram and neural language models.
focus: Part I (Discrete Noiseless Systems: entropy, the approximations to English, source coding); Part II (The Discrete Channel with Noise: equivocation, capacity, the fundamental theorem). Part V (The Rate for a Continuous Source) introduces rate–distortion; skim Part IV (The Continuous Channel) on a first pass.

citation: Shannon, C. E., & Weaver, W. (1949). *The Mathematical Theory of Communication*. University of Illinois Press (paperback 1963).
why: The book reprints Shannon 1948 with an introductory essay by Weaver for general readers. Weaver's essay is where communication studies picked up the "Shannon–Weaver model" and his three levels of communication problems (technical, semantic, effectiveness). For a communication scholar it shows exactly where the engineering theory stops and the metaphor begins.
focus: Weaver's introductory essay; the Shannon paper itself is covered by shannon-1948-mathematical.
translation: 『通信の数学的理論』 クロード・E・シャノン, ワレン・ウィーバー著, 植松友彦訳, ちくま学芸文庫 (筑摩書房), 2009.

citation: Pierce, J. R. (1980). *An Introduction to Information Theory: Symbols, Signals and Noise* (2nd rev. ed.). Dover Publications. xii + 305 pp. (First published as *Symbols, Signals and Noise*, 1961.)
why: Pierce was Shannon's colleague at Bell Labs. He explains entropy, coding, channel capacity and the limits of the theory with almost no formulas, and he is careful about what "information" does *not* mean (meaning, value). It is the classic first read for building intuition before the mathematics.

citation: Stone, J. V. (2022). *Information Theory: A Tutorial Introduction* (2nd ed.). Sebtel Press. ISBN 9781739672706. (1st ed. 2015.)
why: A worked-example on-ramp written by a University of Sheffield psychologist. It is rigorous but gentle, and it bridges Pierce's prose and Cover & Thomas's proofs. The 2nd edition adds chapters on rate–distortion theory and transfer entropy, the latter relevant for information flow between time series (e.g., between media and public attention).
focus: whole. Start with the author's free condensed tutorial (arXiv:1802.05968), which follows the book's arc.
access: need-copy (free condensed version by the author: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.05968)

citation: Gleick, J. (2011). *The Information: A History, a Theory, a Flood*. Pantheon. ISBN 9780375423727.
why: A narrative history running from talking drums and the telegraph to Shannon, Kolmogorov and the information flood. It gives the cultural and intellectual context the textbooks skip. Futrell's information-theoretic linguistics course assigns its Shannon chapter (Ch. 7) as the introduction.
focus: Ch. 7 (the Shannon chapter, as assigned in Futrell's syllabus); then the rest as leisure reading.
translation: 『インフォメーション―情報技術の人類史―』 ジェイムズ・グリック著, 楡井浩一訳, 新潮社, 2013.

citation: Cover, T. M., & Thomas, J. A. (2006). *Elements of Information Theory* (2nd ed.). Wiley-Interscience. ISBN 9780471241959.
why: The standard graduate textbook, used or recommended by both the MIT 6.441 and Stanford EE376A syllabi. Its coverage is unusually broad for a social scientist: gambling, statistics, maximum entropy, Kolmogorov complexity and portfolio theory each get a chapter. The precise definitions and inequalities here are what you cite in papers.
focus: Ch. 2 (Entropy, Relative Entropy, and Mutual Information), 3 (AEP), 5 (Data Compression), 6 (Gambling and Data Compression), 7 (Channel Capacity), 10 (Rate Distortion Theory), 11 (Information Theory and Statistics), 12 (Maximum Entropy), 14 (Kolmogorov Complexity), 16 (Information Theory and Portfolio Theory).
translation: 『情報理論 基礎と広がり』 T.M.カバー, J.A.トーマス著, 山本博資・古賀弘樹・有村光晴ほか訳, 共立出版, 2012.

citation: MacKay, D. J. C. (2003). *Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms*. Cambridge University Press. ISBN 9780521642989.
why: It unites information theory with Bayesian inference and machine learning, which is the best fit for a computational social scientist. MacKay teaches through puzzles and exercises, and the book is free to view on screen from the author's site. His Cambridge course lecture videos accompany it: https://www.inference.org.uk/itprnn_lectures/
focus: Ch. 1 (Introduction to Information Theory), 2 (Probability, Entropy, and Inference), 4 (The Source Coding Theorem), 5 (Symbol Codes), 6 (Stream Codes), 8 (Dependent Random Variables), 9 (Communication over a Noisy Channel), 10 (The Noisy-Channel Coding Theorem), 28 (Model Comparison and Occam's Razor), 33 (Variational Methods).

citation: Polyanskiy, Y., & Wu, Y. (2025). *Information Theory: From Coding to Learning* (1st ed.). Cambridge University Press. DOI 10.1017/9781108966351.
why: The modern graduate treatment, grown out of MIT 6.441. It pairs classical Shannon theory with f-divergences, variational characterizations and statistical learning (hypothesis testing, minimax lower bounds). Use it to look up a rigorous modern statement of a result.
focus: Part I (Information measures: Ch. 1 Entropy, 2 Divergence, 3 Mutual information); Part VI (Statistical applications) for learning-theory links.
access: free: https://people.lids.mit.edu/yp/homepage/data/itbook-export.pdf (authors' prepublication version, free for personal use)

citation: 3Blue1Brown [G. Sanderson] (2022, Feb 6). *Solving Wordle using information theory*. YouTube / 3blue1brown.com lesson.
why: Probably the best visual intuition pump for entropy as "expected bits of information from a guess." It builds a Wordle solver that picks the guess with maximal expected information. Watch it before or alongside Pierce.

citation: Kullback, S., & Leibler, R. A. (1951). *On Information and Sufficiency*. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 22(1), 79–86. DOI 10.1214/aoms/1177729694.
why: It introduces the "mean information for discrimination" now called KL divergence (relative entropy) and ties it to sufficient statistics. KL is the quantity behind maximum likelihood, cross-entropy loss, variational inference, RLHF's KL penalty and model comparison. The paper is short and readable.

citation: Nielsen, F. (2020). *An Elementary Introduction to Information Geometry*. Entropy, 22(10), 1100. DOI 10.3390/e22101100.
why: An open-access tutorial on the geometric view of families of probability distributions: the Fisher metric, dual connections and Bregman divergences. It shows that KL divergence is locally a squared distance, and it is the shortest legitimate route into Amari-style information geometry.
focus: whole (read after Cover & Thomas Ch. 2 and 11).

citation: Tishby, N., Pereira, F. C., & Bialek, W. (2000). *The information bottleneck method*. arXiv:physics/0004057.
why: It defines "relevant information" as finding a compressed code for X that keeps as much information as possible about Y, a rate–distortion problem where the distortion measure is itself information. This framework now underlies work on efficient semantic categories (Zaslavsky et al., assigned in Futrell's course) and on representation learning.

citation: Kolmogorov, A. N. (1965). Three approaches to the definition of the concept "quantity of information." *Problemy Peredachi Informatsii*, 1(1), 3–11. English translation: *Three approaches to the quantitative definition of information*. International Journal of Computer Mathematics, 2(1–4), 157–168 (1968). DOI 10.1080/00207166808803030.
why: Kolmogorov contrasts combinatorial, probabilistic (Shannon) and algorithmic definitions of information. The algorithmic one, the length of the shortest program that outputs an object, measures information in a single object without any probability distribution. It is the primary source for Kolmogorov complexity.
access: need-copy (English); the Russian original is free at https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/ppi68

citation: Rissanen, J. (1978). *Modeling by shortest data description*. Automatica, 14(5), 465–471. DOI 10.1016/0005-1098(78)90005-5.
why: This founding paper of MDL argues that the best model is the one giving the shortest total description of the model plus the data encoded with it. It turns Occam's razor into a computable criterion and shows that model selection is data compression.

citation: Grünwald, P. D. (2007). *The Minimum Description Length Principle*. MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-07281-6. 570 pp.
why: The definitive modern treatment of MDL. It covers crude two-part codes, refined MDL, normalized maximum likelihood and the relations to Bayes and prequential prediction. It is the right depth for judging model-selection claims (e.g., MDL-based community detection or topic-number selection).
focus: Part I (Ch. 1 Learning, Regularity, and Compression; Ch. 2–5 preliminaries and Crude Two-Part Code MDL); Ch. 14 (MDL Model Selection); Ch. 17 (MDL in Context).
access: need-copy (Ch. 1 and Ch. 17 are free samples at https://homepages.cwi.nl/~pdg/book/book.html; the author's free 80-page tutorial is https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0406077)

citation: Li, M., & Vitányi, P. (2019). *An Introduction to Kolmogorov Complexity and Its Applications* (4th ed.). Springer, Texts in Computer Science. DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-11298-1.
why: The encyclopedic reference on algorithmic information: plain and prefix complexity, algorithmic probability (Solomonoff), inductive reasoning and the incompressibility method. Consult it when you need a precise statement rather than reading it cover to cover.

citation: Rosvall, M., & Bergstrom, C. T. (2008). *Maps of random walks on complex networks reveal community structure*. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 105(4), 1118–1123. DOI 10.1073/pnas.0706851105.
why: The "map equation" (Infomap) finds network communities by minimizing the description length of a random walk under a two-level code. It is MDL and Shannon source coding applied directly to network science, the most direct bridge from this field to Kunhao's own network work.

citation: Jaynes, E. T. (1957). *Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics*. Physical Review, 106(4), 620–630. DOI 10.1103/PhysRev.106.620. (Part II: Physical Review, 108, 171.)
why: Jaynes recasts statistical mechanics as inference. Given only some constraints (e.g., average energy), the least-biased distribution is the one with maximum entropy, which yields the Gibbs/Boltzmann distribution. This MaxEnt principle underlies logit models, exponential-family models and ERGMs.
focus: the opening sections that set out the maximum-entropy argument, before the physics applications.

citation: Jaynes, E. T. (2003). *Probability Theory: The Logic of Science* (G. L. Bretthorst, Ed.). Cambridge University Press. DOI 10.1017/CBO9780511790423.
why: Jaynes's magnum opus derives probability as extended logic and places maximum entropy inside Bayesian reasoning. It is polemical and deep. This catalog uses it for the entropy-principle and communication-theory chapters; the Bayesian canon will use more of it.
focus: Ch. 11 (Discrete prior probabilities: the entropy principle); Ch. 22 (Introduction to communication theory); Ch. 1–2 for the framing.

citation: Landauer, R. (1961). *Irreversibility and Heat Generation in the Computing Process*. IBM Journal of Research and Development, 5(3), 183–191. DOI 10.1147/rd.53.0183.
why: Landauer shows that logically irreversible operations, such as erasing a bit, must dissipate at least kT ln 2 of heat ("information is physical"). This principle resolves Maxwell's demon and fixes the physical meaning of Shannon/Gibbs entropy.

citation: Shannon, C. E. (1951). *Prediction and Entropy of Printed English*. Bell System Technical Journal, 30(1), 50–64. DOI 10.1002/j.1538-7305.1951.tb01366.x.
why: Shannon used human subjects guessing the next letter to bound the entropy of English at about 1 bit per letter. This is the ancestor of language modeling and of today's perplexity and surprisal metrics. Futrell's information-theoretic linguistics syllabus assigns it.

citation: Kelly, J. L., Jr. (1956). *A New Interpretation of Information Rate*. Bell System Technical Journal, 35(4), 917–926. DOI 10.1002/j.1538-7305.1956.tb03809.x.
why: A gambler with a noisy private tip can grow wealth exponentially at a rate equal to the mutual information of the tip channel. This gives "information rate" an economic meaning and founded the Kelly criterion and log-optimal investing. Cover & Thomas Ch. 6 and 16 develop it.

citation: Gibson, E., Futrell, R., Piantadosi, S. T., Dautriche, I., Mahowald, K., Bergen, L., & Levy, R. (2019). *How Efficiency Shapes Human Language*. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 23(5), 389–407. DOI 10.1016/j.tics.2019.02.003.
why: The synthesis review of information-theoretic linguistics. It argues that lexicon, syntax and processing are shaped by efficient communication under noise and effort constraints (word length vs. predictability, surprisal, dependency-length minimization, information-bottleneck semantics). It is the gateway from Shannon to cognition and to evaluating LLMs as models of language.

citation: Sims, C. A. (2003). *Implications of rational inattention*. Journal of Monetary Economics, 50(3), 665–690. DOI 10.1016/S0304-3932(03)00029-1.
why: Sims models economic agents as having finite Shannon channel capacity for processing information, which explains sluggish, smoothed responses to news. Rational inattention is now the main way economics brings information theory into models of attention, which is relevant to attention-fatigue and media-attention research.

citation: Adriaans, P. (2012; substantive revision 2023). *Information*. In E. N. Zalta (Ed.), *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*.
why: A philosophical map of the concept of information: Shannon's probabilistic measure, Kolmogorov's program-length measure, and the problems of semantic information and meaning. Use it to keep the technical and everyday senses of "information" apart, especially when writing on misinformation.
focus: §1 (Concepts of Information); §4.2 (Shannon); §4.3 (Solomonoff, Kolmogorov, Chaitin); §6.4 (Model Selection and Data Compression); §6.6 (Logic and Semantic Information).

citation: Sanderson, G. (2016). *Essence of Linear Algebra* (video series: preview + Chapters 1–16). 3Blue1Brown, YouTube.
why: This series treats a matrix as a transformation of space, not a grid of numbers. Determinants become area or volume scaling factors, matrix products become compositions of transformations, and eigenvectors become the directions that stay on their own line. It is the standard geometric warm-up recommended alongside almost every course, and it builds the intuition that formal texts assume and never draw.
focus: Ch. 1 "Vectors"; Ch. 2 "Linear combinations, span, and basis vectors"; Ch. 3 "Linear transformations and matrices"; Ch. 4 "Matrix multiplication as composition"; Ch. 6 "The determinant"; Ch. 7 "Inverse matrices, column space and null space"; Ch. 9 "Dot products and duality"; Ch. 13 "Change of basis"; Ch. 14 "Eigenvectors and eigenvalues"; Ch. 16 "Abstract vector spaces".
verified: https://www.3blue1brown.com/lessons/eola-preview (series dated Aug 2016); chapter titles from the YouTube playlist above.

citation: Strang, G. (2010). *18.06 Linear Algebra, Spring 2010* [video lectures and course materials]. MIT OpenCourseWare.
why: These are the most widely watched linear algebra lectures in the world. Strang organises the subject around the "four fundamental subspaces" and the column picture of Ax = b. The course reaches graphs and incidence matrices, Markov matrices, and the SVD early, which is exactly what a network scientist needs.
focus: Lecture 1 "The geometry of linear equations"; L10 "The four fundamental subspaces"; L11 "Matrix spaces; rank 1; small world graphs"; L12 "Graphs, networks, incidence matrices"; L14–16 (orthogonality, projections, least squares); L21–22 (eigenvalues, diagonalization and powers of A); L24 "Markov matrices; fourier series"; L25 and L27 (positive definite matrices); L29 "Singular value decomposition"; L31 "Change of basis; image compression".

citation: Strang, G. (2023). *Introduction to Linear Algebra* (6th ed.). Wellesley-Cambridge Press. ISBN 978-1-7331466-7-8.
why: This is the textbook behind 18.06. The 6th edition rebuilds the subject around the factorizations A = CR, LU, QR, QΛQᵀ, and UΣVᵀ, so every topic becomes a way of factoring data. New chapters connect directly to optimization and learning from data.
focus: 1.3 "Matrices and Their Column Spaces"; 1.4 "Matrix Multiplication AB and CR"; 3.5 "Dimensions of the Four Subspaces"; 4.2 "Projections onto Lines and Subspaces"; 4.3 "Least Squares Approximations"; 6.1–6.3 (eigenvalues, diagonalizing, symmetric positive definite); Ch. 7 "The Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)" (7.1–7.3, including PCA by the SVD); 9.4 "Linear Programming, Game Theory, and Duality".
access: need-copy (free sample sections 1.4, 2.2, 3.5, 6.1 and the outline are on the author's site: https://math.mit.edu/~gs/linearalgebra/ila6/indexila6.html)

citation: Strang, G. (2020). *Linear Algebra for Everyone*. Wellesley-Cambridge Press. ISBN 978-1-7331466-3-0.
why: This is Strang's shorter, data-oriented version of the subject. It opens with column-times-row thinking (A = CR) and moves quickly to the SVD and to learning from data. It suits a working scientist who wants Strang's viewpoint without the full 18.06 syllabus.
focus: whole (Sections 1.3 and 1.4 and an SVD image-compression note are free samples on the author's site)

citation: Hiranabe, K. (with the help of G. Strang) (2021; updated 2025). *The Art of Linear Algebra: Graphic Notes on "Linear Algebra for Everyone"*. GitHub repository, 12 pp. PDF.
why: These are visual "cheat-sheet" diagrams of the five matrix factorizations (CR, LU, QR, QΛQᵀ, UΣVᵀ), plus a "Map of Eigenvalues" and a "Matrix World" diagram, made with Strang's blessing. Each factorization becomes a picture of how columns and rows combine, which makes it a good compact review. It is written by a Japanese engineer and has a Japanese version.
focus: whole (12 pages); also "MapofEigenvalues.pdf" and "MatrixWorld.pdf" in the same repository.
translation: Japanese version (The-Art-of-Linear-Algebra-j.pdf) and Chinese version (The-Art-of-Linear-Algebra-zh-CN.pdf) in the same repository.

citation: Axler, S. (2024). *Linear Algebra Done Right* (4th ed.). Springer, Undergraduate Texts in Mathematics. Open Access (CC BY-NC). https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-41026-0
why: Axler develops the theory through linear maps and operators, with determinants postponed to the end, so eigenvalues, the spectral theorem, and the SVD are proved from structure rather than computation. It is the standard proof-based text (adopted at 375+ universities). It is the place to learn *why* symmetric matrices have orthonormal eigenbases and *why* the SVD exists.
focus: 3B "Null Spaces and Ranges" (Fundamental Theorem of Linear Maps); 3D "Invertibility and Isomorphisms"; 3F "Duality"; 5A–5D (invariant subspaces, minimal polynomial, upper-triangular matrices, diagonalizable operators); 6B "Orthonormal Bases"; 6C "Orthogonal Complements and Minimization Problems"; 7B "Spectral Theorem"; 7C "Positive Operators"; 7E "Singular Value Decomposition"; 7F "Consequences of Singular Value Decomposition".
translation: Chinese: 《线性代数应该这样学（第四版）》, trans. 吴俊达, 何阳, free PDF at https://linear.axler.net/LADR4eChinese.pdf (a print Chinese translation of the 3rd ed., 《线性代数应该这样学（第3版）》, also exists).

citation: Halmos, P. R. (1958). *Finite-Dimensional Vector Spaces* (2nd ed.). Van Nostrand. Reprinted 1974, Springer-Verlag, Undergraduate Texts in Mathematics, viii + 200 pp. ISBN 0-387-90093-4.
why: Halmos wrote this classic to treat finite-dimensional spaces with the methods of Hilbert-space operator theory. It teaches linear algebra as a theory of transformations and inner products that carries over to infinite dimensions. Its short numbered sections are a model of mathematical exposition.
focus: Part I "Spaces"; Part II "Transformations"; Part III "Orthogonality".

citation: Hoffman, K., & Kunze, R. (1971). *Linear Algebra* (2nd ed.). Prentice-Hall, viii + 407 pp.
why: This is the traditional rigorous honors text, covering canonical forms (rational and Jordan), bilinear forms, and modules over polynomial rings. Use it as the reference when you need the full algebraic structure theory that Axler deliberately streamlines.

citation: Boyd, S., & Vandenberghe, L. (2018). *Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra: Vectors, Matrices, and Least Squares*. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108583664
why: This book uses only vectors, matrices, and least squares, and from that small toolkit it gets clustering (k-means), regression, classification, linear dynamical systems, and constrained fitting. It is the textbook for Stanford ENGR108. It shows how far plain linear algebra goes in data work, and it has Julia and Python companions.
focus: Ch. 3 "Norm and distance"; Ch. 4 "Clustering"; Ch. 7 "Matrix examples"; Ch. 9 "Linear dynamical systems"; Ch. 12 "Least squares"; Ch. 13 "Least squares data fitting"; Ch. 14 "Least squares classification"; Ch. 15 "Multi-objective least squares".

citation: Deisenroth, M. P., Faisal, A. A., & Ong, C. S. (2020). *Mathematics for Machine Learning*. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108679930
why: This book is a bridge from linear algebra and analytic geometry to ML. Inner products, projections, and matrix decompositions are developed specifically to explain regression, PCA, GMMs, and SVMs. Its "projection perspective" on PCA and its reading of maximum likelihood as orthogonal projection are especially good for intuition.
focus: Ch. 2 "Linear Algebra"; Ch. 3 "Analytic Geometry" (3.8 "Orthogonal Projections", 3.9 "Rotations"); Ch. 4 "Matrix Decompositions" (4.2, 4.4, 4.5 "Singular Value Decomposition", 4.6 "Matrix Approximation", 4.7 "Matrix Phylogeny"); 9.4 "Maximum Likelihood as Orthogonal Projection"; Ch. 10 "Dimensionality Reduction with Principal Component Analysis".

citation: Strang, G. (2018). *18.065 Matrix Methods in Data Analysis, Signal Processing, and Machine Learning, Spring 2018* [video lectures]. MIT OpenCourseWare. Textbook: Strang, G. (2019). *Linear Algebra and Learning from Data*. Wellesley-Cambridge Press. ISBN 978-0-692-19638-0.
why: This is Strang's sequel to 18.06, aimed at data science. It covers the SVD and the Eckart–Young theorem, the four ways to solve least squares, randomized linear algebra, graph Laplacians and clustering, and the linear algebra of deep learning. The course videos are free; the book is the course text.
focus: Lectures 6 "Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)", 7 "Eckart-Young: The Closest Rank k Matrix to A", 9 "Four Ways to Solve Least Squares Problems", 13 "Randomized Matrix Multiplication", 35 "Finding Clusters in Graphs". Book: Part I (I.1–I.9, ending with "Principal Components and the Best Low Rank Matrix"); II.4 "Randomized Linear Algebra"; IV.6 "Graphs and Laplacians and Kirchhoff's Laws"; IV.7 "Clustering by Spectral Methods and k-means"; V.6 "Markov Chains".
access: free: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-065-matrix-methods-in-data-analysis-signal-processing-and-machine-learning-spring-2018/ (book: need-copy; TOC and sample sections at https://math.mit.edu/~gs/learningfromdata/)

citation: Trefethen, L. N., & Bau, D., III (1997). *Numerical Linear Algebra*. SIAM. ISBN 978-0-89871-361-9. 25th Anniversary ed., SIAM, 2022, https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9781611977165
why: This is the graduate standard (required text for MIT 18.335J). It is written as 40 short lectures that put the SVD at the centre from Lecture 4 onward. It explains what numpy/LAPACK actually do (QR, Householder, eigenvalue algorithms, Krylov methods) and why conditioning and stability decide whether a computed answer can be trusted.
focus: Part I "Fundamentals" (Lectures 1–5, incl. 4 "The Singular Value Decomposition", 5 "More on the SVD"); Part II "QR Factorization and Least Squares" (6–11); Lectures 12 "Conditioning and Condition Numbers", 14 "Stability"; 27 "Rayleigh Quotient, Inverse Iteration"; 33 "The Arnoldi Iteration"; 36 "The Lanczos Iteration"; 38 "Conjugate Gradients".

citation: Golub, G. H., & Van Loan, C. F. (2013). *Matrix Computations* (4th ed.). Johns Hopkins University Press, Johns Hopkins Studies in the Mathematical Sciences, xxi + 756 pp. ISBN 978-1-4214-0794-4.
why: This is the reference work of numerical linear algebra, the book to check for the algorithm, its cost, and its error bounds. The 4th edition adds large-scale SVD, fast transforms, multigrid, and tensor computations.

citation: Pearson, K. (1901). LIII. On lines and planes of closest fit to systems of points in space. *The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science*, 2(11), 559–572. https://doi.org/10.1080/14786440109462720
why: This is the geometric origin of PCA. Pearson asks for the line or plane that minimizes *perpendicular* distances to a point cloud, not vertical ones as in regression. The answer is the principal axes of the correlation ellipsoid, and this "best-fitting subspace" picture is still the clearest intuition for PCA.

citation: Hotelling, H. (1933). Analysis of a complex of statistical variables into principal components. *Journal of Educational Psychology*, 24(6), 417–441. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0071325
why: Hotelling named "principal components" and framed them as the variance-maximizing eigenvectors of a correlation matrix, computed by iteration. This gives the statistical (maximum-variance) view that complements Pearson's geometric one. It came out of psychometrics, like much of early multivariate linear algebra.

citation: Eckart, C., & Young, G. (1936). The approximation of one matrix by another of lower rank. *Psychometrika*, 1(3), 211–218. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02288367
why: This paper proves that truncating the SVD gives the best rank-k approximation of a matrix in least squares. It is the theorem underneath PCA, LSA, image compression, recommender systems, and LoRA-style low-rank adaptation. Strang devotes a full 18.065 lecture to it.

citation: Brin, S., & Page, L. (1998). The anatomy of a large-scale hypertextual Web search engine. *Computer Networks and ISDN Systems*, 30(1–7), 107–117. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0169-7552(98)00110-X
why: This is the founding Google paper. It introduces PageRank as the stationary distribution of a "random surfer" with damping, which turns link structure into importance scores. Read it for the original framing and Section 2.1; read Bryan & Leise for the linear algebra.

citation: Bryan, K., & Leise, T. (2006). The $25,000,000,000 eigenvector: The linear algebra behind Google. *SIAM Review*, 48(3), 569–581. https://doi.org/10.1137/050623280
why: This is the canonical teaching exposition of PageRank as an eigenvector problem. It shows why the raw link matrix can have a non-unique dominant eigenvector, how the damping/teleportation fix guarantees uniqueness (Perron–Frobenius), and why the power method converges at a rate set by the second eigenvalue. It is one of the best single examples of eigenvectors applied to networks.
focus: 2 "Developing a formula to rank pages"; 3 "A remedy for dim(V1(A)) > 1"; 4 "Computing the Importance Score Eigenvector".

citation: Deerwester, S., Dumais, S. T., Furnas, G. W., Landauer, T. K., & Harshman, R. (1990). Indexing by latent semantic analysis. *Journal of the American Society for Information Science*, 41(6), 391–407. https://doi.org/10.1002/(SICI)1097-4571(199009)41:6<391::AID-ASI1>3.0.CO;2-9
why: LSA applies a truncated SVD to a term–document matrix so that words and documents live in one low-dimensional "semantic" space where synonyms end up near each other. It is the direct ancestor of word embeddings and of topic-style text analysis in computational social science.
focus: 3.2 "The choice of method for uncovering latent semantic structure"; 4 "SVD or two-mode factor analysis".

citation: Bonacich, P. (1987). Power and centrality: A family of measures. *American Journal of Sociology*, 92(5), 1170–1182. https://doi.org/10.1086/228631
why: Bonacich defines c(β) = α(I − βA)⁻¹A1, a family of centralities indexed by β. Positive β gives eigenvector-like centrality (being connected to the well-connected); negative β gives "power" in exchange networks (being connected to the *poorly* connected). It is the sociological anchor for the claim that network centralities are matrix functions.
