citation: Turk, M., & Pentland, A. (1991). Eigenfaces for recognition. *Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience*, 3(1), 71–86. https://doi.org/10.1162/jocn.1991.3.1.71
why: PCA applied to face images gives "eigenfaces": a few basis images whose combinations reconstruct and recognize faces. It is the most famous visual demonstration that high-dimensional data often lies near a low-dimensional subspace.

citation: von Luxburg, U. (2007). A tutorial on spectral clustering. *Statistics and Computing*, 17(4), 395–416. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11222-007-9033-z
why: This is the standard tutorial on graph Laplacians (unnormalized and normalized) and on why their bottom eigenvectors reveal clusters. It derives the result from three viewpoints: relaxed graph cuts, random walks, and perturbation theory. It is the most direct link from linear algebra to community detection.
focus: sections "Graph Laplacians and their basic properties", "Spectral Clustering Algorithms", "Graph cut point of view", "Random walks point of view", "Practical details".

citation: Spielman, D. A. (2025). *Spectral and Algebraic Graph Theory* (incomplete draft, dated April 2, 2025). Yale University, author's website.
why: This book grew out of Spielman's Yale spectral graph theory lecture notes. It teaches graphs through their matrices, using physical metaphors (springs, resistor networks, random walks) and theorems such as Courant–Fischer, Perron–Frobenius, and Cheeger's inequality. It is the deepest free text connecting eigenvalues to network structure, partitioning, and fast Laplacian solvers.
focus: Part I chs. 1–4 (incl. 2 "Eigenvalues and Optimization: The Courant-Fischer Theorem", 3 "The Laplacian and Graph Drawing", 4 "Adjacency matrices, Eigenvalue Interlacing, and the Perron-Frobenius Theorem"); 10 "Random Walks on Graphs"; 11 "Walks, Springs, and Resistor Networks"; 20 "Graph Partitioning"; 21 "Cheeger's Inequality"; 23 "Spectral Partitioning in a Stochastic Block Model".

citation: Mikolov, T., Yih, W., & Zweig, G. (2013). Linguistic regularities in continuous space word representations. In *Proceedings of NAACL-HLT 2013* (pp. 746–751). Association for Computational Linguistics.
why: This paper shows that learned word vectors encode relations as roughly constant *offsets*, so analogies can be solved by vector arithmetic (king − man + woman ≈ queen) and cosine similarity. It is the founding demonstration of "meaning as geometry" behind the linear-representation ideas in LLM interpretability. It cross-references the LLM field.

strand: Prehistory — from n-grams to word vectors
citation: Bengio, Y., Ducharme, R., Vincent, P., & Jauvin, C. (2003). *A Neural Probabilistic Language Model*. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 3, 1137–1155.
why: This paper replaces counting n-grams with a neural network that learns a dense vector for each word together with the probability of the next word. It is the direct ancestor of every modern LM: it learns embeddings, shares statistical strength across similar words, and is trained to predict the next token. Read it to see that the core idea predates deep learning hardware by a decade.

strand: Prehistory — from n-grams to word vectors
citation: Mikolov, T., Chen, K., Corrado, G., & Dean, J. (2013). *Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space*. ICLR 2013 Workshop. arXiv:1301.3781.
why: This paper introduces the CBOW and skip-gram architectures (word2vec), which made it cheap to learn word vectors from billions of tokens. It also introduces the semantic/syntactic analogy test set, which turned "meaning as geometry" into something you can measure. It is the starting point for the linear-algebra view of meaning that later interpretability work builds on.

strand: Prehistory — from n-grams to word vectors
citation: Mikolov, T., Sutskever, I., Chen, K., Corrado, G., & Dean, J. (2013). *Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality*. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 26 (NeurIPS 2013). arXiv:1310.4546.
why: This is the companion paper that made skip-gram practical. It adds negative sampling, subsampling of frequent words and phrase tokens, and shows that vectors compose additively. Negative sampling was later shown to implicitly factorize a pointwise-mutual-information matrix, which makes it the cleanest bridge from LMs to information theory and linear algebra.

strand: Architecture — attention and the Transformer family
citation: Bahdanau, D., Cho, K., & Bengio, Y. (2015). *Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate*. ICLR 2015. arXiv:1409.0473.
why: This paper introduces (additive) attention. Instead of squeezing a whole sentence into one vector, the decoder learns a soft, differentiable "alignment" over all encoder states. Every Transformer is a generalization of this move, and the alignment heatmaps here were the first interpretable view inside a neural translator.

strand: Architecture — attention and the Transformer family
citation: Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., Uszkoreit, J., Jones, L., Gomez, A. N., Kaiser, Ł., & Polosukhin, I. (2017). *Attention Is All You Need*. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30 (NeurIPS 2017). arXiv:1706.03762.
why: This paper drops recurrence entirely and builds the model from scaled dot-product self-attention, multiple heads, positional encodings, residual connections and feed-forward blocks. Because the result parallelizes well, it is the architecture that made scaling possible. Every model in this canon is a variant of it.
focus: whole (short; the model-architecture section is the heart)

strand: Architecture — attention and the Transformer family
citation: Devlin, J., Chang, M.-W., Lee, K., & Toutanova, K. (2019). *BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding*. Proceedings of NAACL-HLT 2019, Vol. 1, 4171–4186. DOI:10.18653/v1/N19-1423.
why: BERT is the encoder-only, masked-language-model branch of the family. It established "pretrain, then fine-tune" as the default NLP workflow. Most of the classifier and embedding tools used in computational social science, such as fine-tuned stance and frame classifiers and sentence embeddings, descend from it, so it is the baseline against which LLM surrogate labeling is judged.

strand: Architecture — attention and the Transformer family
citation: Radford, A., Wu, J., Child, R., Luan, D., Amodei, D., & Sutskever, I. (2019). *Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners*. OpenAI technical report.
why: This paper argues that a large enough next-token predictor trained on diverse web text learns tasks implicitly. It shows zero-shot summarization (triggered by appending "TL;DR:"), translation and question answering with no task-specific training. It is the conceptual pivot from "pretrain, then fine-tune" to "the prompt is the task specification." It builds on the 2018 GPT-1 report, which is not listed separately.

strand: Architecture — attention and the Transformer family
citation: Brown, T. B., Mann, B., Ryder, N., Subbiah, M., et al. (2020). *Language Models are Few-Shot Learners*. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (NeurIPS 2020). arXiv:2005.14165.
why: GPT-3 (175B parameters) showed that in-context few-shot learning, where the model learns from examples placed in the prompt without any gradient updates, improves smoothly with scale. This created the modern prompting paradigm and the "LLM as general-purpose annotator" idea behind surrogate labeling. The long limitations and broader-impacts sections are worth reading too.
focus: whole is very long; prioritize the introduction (zero/one/few-shot framing), then the limitations and broader-impacts sections

citation: Kaplan, J., McCandlish, S., Henighan, T., Brown, T. B., Chess, B., Child, R., Gray, S., Radford, A., Wu, J., & Amodei, D. (2020). *Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models*. arXiv:2001.08361.
why: This paper shows that cross-entropy loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters, data and compute, across many orders of magnitude. That turned model building into a forecasting exercise. It is the empirical basis for "just scale it" and a good place to think about loss as information (bits per token).
focus: whole (the summary of results and the main power-law figures first)

citation: Hoffmann, J., Borgeaud, S., Mensch, A., et al. (2022). *Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models*. arXiv:2203.15556. Published at NeurIPS 2022 under the title "An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal Large Language Model Training".
why: This paper corrects Kaplan's allocation rule: for a fixed compute budget, parameters and training tokens should grow roughly in equal proportion. Its 70B "Chinchilla" model outperformed much larger models trained on fewer tokens. It is the canonical lesson that scaling laws depend on how the experiments are designed.

citation: Ouyang, L., Wu, J., Jiang, X., et al. (2022). *Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback*. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (NeurIPS 2022). arXiv:2203.02155.
why: InstructGPT is the standard recipe behind chat assistants: supervised fine-tuning, then a reward model trained on human pairwise preferences, then PPO with a KL penalty that keeps the model close to the pretrained one. Its headline result is that outputs from a 1.3B InstructGPT were preferred to those of 175B GPT-3. It extends Christiano et al. (2017) on RL from human preferences and is central to the LLM-safety thread.

citation: Bai, Y., Kadavath, S., Kundu, S., Askell, A., et al. (2022). *Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback*. arXiv:2212.08073.
why: This paper replaces human harmlessness labels with AI feedback guided by a short written "constitution" of principles. The model critiques and revises its own outputs, then RL from AI feedback (RLAIF) follows. It is the canonical statement of principle-based, scalable oversight, and it bears directly on how safety behavior can differ across languages and cultures.

citation: Rafailov, R., Sharma, A., Mitchell, E., Ermon, S., Manning, C. D., & Finn, C. (2023). *Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model*. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (NeurIPS 2023). arXiv:2305.18290.
why: DPO derives the closed-form optimum of KL-regularized reward maximization and rewrites RLHF as a simple classification loss on preference pairs, with no reward model and no RL loop. It is the cleanest mathematical view of what RLHF is doing (a Bradley–Terry model plus a Gibbs-form policy) and is now a standard post-training method.
focus: whole (the derivation of the DPO objective is the core)

strand: Capabilities, reasoning and the emergence debate
citation: Wei, J., Wang, X., Schuurmans, D., Bosma, M., Ichter, B., Xia, F., Chi, E., Le, Q., & Zhou, D. (2022). *Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models*. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (NeurIPS 2022). arXiv:2201.11903.
why: Few-shot examples that include written-out intermediate reasoning steps sharply improve multi-step arithmetic and commonsense reasoning in large models. PaLM 540B reached state of the art on GSM8K this way. This is the origin of "let the model think in tokens," which leads to today's reasoning models, and it is a natural object for theory-of-mind and philosophy-of-explanation questions.

strand: Capabilities, reasoning and the emergence debate
citation: Wei, J., Tay, Y., Bommasani, R., Raffel, C., Zoph, B., Borgeaud, S., Yogatama, D., Bosma, M., Zhou, D., Metzler, D., Chi, E. H., Hashimoto, T., Vinyals, O., Liang, P., Dean, J., & Fedus, W. (2022). *Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models*. Transactions on Machine Learning Research. arXiv:2206.07682.
why: This paper defines an "emergent ability" as one that is absent in smaller models and present in larger ones, so it cannot be extrapolated from small-scale trends. It catalogues many examples across benchmarks. Read it together with Schaeffer et al. as one debate.

strand: Capabilities, reasoning and the emergence debate
citation: Schaeffer, R., Miranda, B., & Koyejo, S. (2023). *Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?* Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (NeurIPS 2023). arXiv:2304.15004.
why: This paper argues that many "emergent" jumps come from the researcher's choice of metric: nonlinear or discontinuous metrics such as exact match turn smooth per-token improvement into apparent sudden leaps. It is a methodological lesson about measurement that applies directly to LLM evaluation in social science.

strand: Capabilities, reasoning and the emergence debate
citation: Xie, S. M., Raghunathan, A., Liang, P., & Ma, T. (2022). *An Explanation of In-context Learning as Implicit Bayesian Inference*. ICLR 2022. arXiv:2111.02080.
why: In a stylized setting where pretraining documents come from a mixture of hidden Markov models, this paper proves that next-token prediction yields in-context learning: the model implicitly infers the latent "concept" shared by the prompt examples. It is the key bridge from LLM behavior to Bayesian theory, and it is on the Princeton COS 597G reading list.
focus: setup and main theorem; synthetic GINC experiments

citation: Elhage, N., Nanda, N., Olsson, C., Henighan, T., Joseph, N., Mann, B., Askell, A., Bai, Y., Chen, A., Conerly, T., et al., & Olah, C. (2021). *A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits*. Transformer Circuits Thread (Anthropic), Dec 22, 2021.
why: This paper rewrites attention-only Transformers as sums of linear paths through a "residual stream." It decomposes each head into a QK circuit (where to attend) and an OV circuit (what to copy), so the model can be read with linear algebra. It is the foundational text of mechanistic interpretability and directly relevant to explainable representation learning.
focus: Summary of Results; Transformer Overview; Zero-Layer; One-Layer Attention-Only; Two-Layer Attention-Only; Induction Heads

citation: Olsson, C., Elhage, N., Nanda, N., Joseph, N., DasSarma, N., Henighan, T., Mann, B., et al., & Olah, C. (2022). *In-context Learning and Induction Heads*. Transformer Circuits Thread (Anthropic), Mar 8, 2022.
why: This paper argues across six lines of evidence that "induction heads," a two-head circuit that completes [A][B] … [A] → [B], account for much of in-context learning. They form during a sudden phase change in training that shows up as a bump in the loss curve. It is a mechanistic counterpart to the Bayesian story in xie-2022-icl.
focus: Key Concepts; Arguments (start with Argument 1, the phase change)

citation: Elhage, N., Hume, T., Olsson, C., Schiefer, N., Henighan, T., et al., & Olah, C. (2022). *Toy Models of Superposition*. Transformer Circuits Thread (Anthropic). arXiv:2209.10652.
why: Small ReLU models show that networks store more sparse features than they have dimensions by packing them into nearly orthogonal directions ("superposition"). The features arrange themselves in regular geometric shapes, and the switch into superposition behaves like a phase change. This explains why single neurons are rarely interpretable and motivates dictionary learning.
focus: Background & Motivation; Demonstrating Superposition; Superposition as a Phase Change; The Geometry of Superposition

citation: Geva, M., Schuster, R., Berant, J., & Levy, O. (2021). *Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories*. Proceedings of EMNLP 2021, 5484–5495. DOI:10.18653/v1/2021.emnlp-main.446.
why: The first FFN matrix acts as "keys" that detect input patterns, and the second acts as "values" that push up particular next-token distributions. This gives a concrete, linear-algebraic account of where factual and lexical knowledge is stored. It complements the attention-centric circuits work.

citation: Templeton, A., Conerly, T., Marcus, J., Lindsey, J., et al., Olah, C., & Henighan, T. (2024). *Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet*. Transformer Circuits Thread (Anthropic), May 21, 2024.
why: This paper scales sparse-autoencoder dictionary learning to a production model and finds millions of interpretable, often multilingual and multimodal features, including safety-relevant ones such as deception and sycophancy. Turning a feature up or down causally steers the model's behavior. It is the state-of-the-art demonstration that the superposition hypothesis can be put to practical use.
focus: Scaling Dictionary Learning to Claude 3 Sonnet; Feature Survey; Safety-Relevant Features; Limitations, Challenges, and Open Problems

citation: Bender, E. M., & Koller, A. (2020). *Climbing towards NLU: On Meaning, Form, and Understanding in the Age of Data*. Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the ACL, 5185–5198. DOI:10.18653/v1/2020.acl-main.463.
why: The paper argues that a system trained only on linguistic form cannot in principle learn meaning, which it defines as the relation between form and communicative intent. It makes the case with the "octopus test" thought experiment. It is the clearest statement of the grounding critique and a direct entry point to the philosophy-of-language canon.

citation: Piantadosi, S. T., & Hill, F. (2022). *Meaning without reference in large language models*. arXiv:2208.02957.
why: This is the direct counterpoint to Bender & Koller. It argues that meaning comes mainly from conceptual role (relations among internal representations) rather than reference, so LLMs may capture important aspects of meaning without grounding. It is short, philosophical and pairs naturally with analytic philosophy of language (inferentialism versus referentialism).

citation: Mahowald, K., Ivanova, A. A., Blank, I. A., Kanwisher, N., Tenenbaum, J. B., & Fedorenko, E. (2024). *Dissociating language and thought in large language models*. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 28(6), 517–540. DOI:10.1016/j.tics.2024.01.011.
why: Drawing on cognitive neuroscience, the authors distinguish formal linguistic competence (grammar, form), which LLMs largely have, from functional competence (reasoning, world knowledge, situation modeling, social reasoning), which is uneven. This framework replaces "do LLMs understand?" with sharper questions and links directly to theory of mind.

citation: Bender, E. M., Gebru, T., McMillan-Major, A., & Shmitchell, S. (2021). *On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots: Can Language Models Be Too Big?* Proceedings of the 2021 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT '21). DOI:10.1145/3442188.3445922.
why: This paper is the agenda-setting critique of scale. It covers environmental and financial cost, undocumented and biased web training data, and the risk that fluent text is mistaken for meaning; it coined the phrase "stochastic parrot." It is essential context for LLM-safety and misinformation research and for the sociology of the field.
access: need-copy (the ACM DL page could not be reached from here to confirm open access; check the DOI through institutional access first)

citation: Argyle, L. P., Busby, E. C., Fulda, N., Gubler, J. R., Rytting, C., & Wingate, D. (2023). *Out of One, Many: Using Language Models to Simulate Human Samples*. Political Analysis, 31(3), 337–351. DOI:10.1017/pan.2023.2.
why: The paper conditions GPT-3 on demographic backstories to create "silicon samples." It introduces "algorithmic fidelity," the degree to which a model's conditional distributions match those of real subpopulations, as the criterion for using LLMs as survey proxies. It is the founding paper of LLM-based simulation of respondents.

citation: Ziems, C., Held, W., Shaikh, O., Chen, J., Zhang, Z., & Yang, D. (2024). *Can Large Language Models Transform Computational Social Science?* Computational Linguistics, 50(1), 237–291. DOI:10.1162/coli_a_00502.
why: This paper systematically benchmarks LLMs zero-shot on many CSS classification and generation tasks across sociology, political science, psychology and history. It concludes that LLMs can augment human annotation but not replace it, and gives practical guidance. It is the reference point for LLM surrogate labeling.
focus: whole (taxonomy of tasks and the recommendations section)

citation: Park, J. S., O'Brien, J. C., Cai, C. J., Morris, M. R., Liang, P., & Bernstein, M. S. (2023). *Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior*. Proceedings of UIST 2023 (ACM). arXiv:2304.03442.
why: The paper builds an agent architecture with memory stream, reflection and planning, and runs 25 LLM agents in a sandbox town, where social behavior such as spreading a party invitation emerges. It is the canonical starting point for LLM-based social simulation and invites comparison with classic agent-based modeling.

citation: Jurafsky, D., & Martin, J. H. (2026). *Speech and Language Processing* (3rd ed., online draft released Aug 19, 2026). Stanford University.
why: This is the standard NLP textbook, rewritten around LLMs. Volume I now reads as an LLM textbook, running from tokens and n-grams through embeddings to transformers and post-training. It is the backbone reading for CS224N-style courses and the best single on-ramp with real depth.
focus: Ch. 3 N-gram Language Models; Ch. 5 Embeddings; Ch. 7 Transformers and Pretraining; Ch. 8 Post-training; Ch. 9 Masked Language Models; Ch. 10 Interpretability

citation: Karpathy, A. (2022–ongoing). *Neural Networks: Zero to Hero* (video lecture series with code).
why: You build everything from scratch in Python: autograd (micrograd), character-level LMs (makemore), a GPT and a BPE tokenizer. For someone who uses Python daily it is the fastest way to get hands-on intuition, so that the papers read as code rather than abstraction.
focus: 1 micrograd; 2 makemore (bigram LM); 3 makemore MLP (≈ Bengio 2003); 7 "Let's build GPT"; 8 "Let's build the GPT Tokenizer"

citation: Prince, S. J. D. (2023). *Understanding Deep Learning*. MIT Press.
why: This is a modern, clearly illustrated deep-learning textbook (free PDF with notebooks) that covers the mathematical background the LLM papers assume: loss functions as likelihoods, optimization, regularization and transformers. It is the preferred modern replacement for Goodfellow et al. (2016) as a reference.
focus: Ch. 12 Transformers; earlier chapters on loss functions and fitting as needed

citation: Clark, W. R., Golder, M., & Golder, S. N. (2017). *Principles of Comparative Politics* (3rd ed.). Thousand Oaks, CA: CQ Press / SAGE.
why: This is the standard introduction to comparative politics with an explicitly game-theoretic, cumulative-science approach. Simple strategic models (exit/voice/loyalty, the state as a protection racket, transition games) run through it alongside cross-national evidence. Its chapter on group decision making covers the Condorcet paradox, Arrow, and the median voter at undergraduate level, which makes it the gentlest way into strand 2.
focus: Ch. 2 "What Is Science?"; Ch. 3 "What Is Politics?"; Ch. 4 "The Origins of the Modern State"; Ch. 6–7 (economic and cultural determinants of democracy); Ch. 11 "Problems with Group Decision Making"; Ch. 13 "Elections and Electoral Systems"; Ch. 15 "Institutional Veto Players".

citation: Shepsle, K. A. (2010). *Analyzing Politics: Rationality, Behavior, and Institutions* (2nd ed.). New York: W. W. Norton. 560 pp.
why: This is the canonical rational-choice primer. It builds rationality, group choice, Arrow's theorem, collective action, and institutions (agenda power, committees, delegation) from first principles with little mathematics. Graduate formal-theory courses still assign it as the scaffold for Arrow and the institutions literature, and it is the best single bridge from game theory to political institutions.
focus: Chs. 3–4 (group choice and Arrow's theorem; assigned for Arrow in UGA POLS 8000); Chs. 5, 6, 11–13, 15 (institutions, as assigned in the same syllabus).

citation: Arrow, K. J. (1951). *Social Choice and Individual Values*. Cowles Commission Monograph No. 12. New York: John Wiley & Sons; London: Chapman & Hall. xi + 99 pp. (2nd ed. 1963; 3rd ed. Yale University Press 2012.)
why: Arrow proves that no rule for aggregating individual rankings into a social ranking can satisfy a few mild-looking conditions at once (unrestricted domain, Pareto, independence of irrelevant alternatives, non-dictatorship). The result moved "what does the public want?" from rhetoric to an axiomatic, provable question. All of social choice theory, and Riker's skepticism about the "will of the people", starts here.
focus: Ch. I "Introduction"; Ch. II "The Nature of Preference and Choice"; Ch. V "The General Possibility Theorem for Social Welfare Functions" (pp. 46–60). The 1951 first edition has Chs. I–VII.
translation: 『社会的選択と個人的評価』長名寛明訳、日本経済新聞社、1977（新版2013）
verified: https://cowles.yale.edu/sites/default/files/2022-09/m12-all.pdf (title page, copyright and contents checked); translation: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/ケネス・アロー

citation: Downs, A. (1957). *An Economic Theory of Democracy*. New York: Harper. Companion article: Downs, A. (1957). An economic theory of political action in a democracy. *Journal of Political Economy*, 65(2), 135–150. doi:10.1086/257897
why: Downs models parties as vote-maximizers and voters as utility-maximizers, and from that derives spatial convergence (the median voter), the role of ideology as an information shortcut, the paradox of voting, and "rational ignorance": information costs more than a single vote is worth. This is the origin of treating citizens' information as an economic problem, which strands 3 and 4 then test.
focus: whole (read the 1957 JPE article first as a 16-page summary)

verified: https://doi.org/10.1086/257897 ; book listed in https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/17-200-graduate-seminar-in-american-politics-i-political-behavior-fall-2016/pages/readings ; translation: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/アンソニー・ダウンズ

citation: Olson, M. (1965). *The Logic of Collective Action: Public Goods and the Theory of Groups*. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press. (2nd printing 1971, with a new preface and appendix.) doi:10.4159/9780674041660
why: Olson shows that shared interest does not produce collective action. Rational individuals free-ride on public goods, so large, diffuse groups (consumers, citizens) are under-organized relative to small, concentrated ones unless there are "selective incentives". This is the micro-foundation of interest-group politics, social movements, and the free-rider problem behind climate action.
focus: Introduction; Ch. I "A Theory of Groups and Organizations"; Ch. II "Group Size and Group Behavior"; Ch. VI "The 'By-Product' and 'Special Interest' Theories".
translation: 『集合行為論――公共財と集団理論』依田博・森脇俊雅訳、ミネルヴァ書房、1983（新装版1996）
verified: https://doi.org/10.4159/9780674041660 ; translation: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/マンサー・オルソン

citation: Hirschman, A. O. (1970). *Exit, Voice, and Loyalty: Responses to Decline in Firms, Organizations, and States*. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press.
why: A short, elegant book on the two feedback channels members have when an organization declines: leaving (exit, the market signal) or complaining (voice, the political signal). Loyalty governs the mix between them. It is a general theory of how information about quality gets back to the people who decide, and it applies directly to platform migration, partisanship, and emigration.
translation: 『離脱・発言・忠誠――企業・組織・国家における衰退への反応』矢野修一訳、ミネルヴァ書房、2005
verified: https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0674276507 ; translation: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/アルバート・O・ハーシュマン

citation: Riker, W. H. (1982). *Liberalism Against Populism: A Confrontation Between the Theory of Democracy and the Theory of Social Choice*. San Francisco: W. H. Freeman. (Reissued Waveland Press, 1988.)
why: Riker draws the political conclusion from Arrow and McKelvey. Because majority outcomes can cycle and be manipulated through agenda control and strategic voting, there is no coherent "popular will" to discover ("populism"). Elections can only let voters remove officials ("liberalism"). The book is canonical as a provocation and anticipates Achen & Bartels' "realist" view.
translation: 『民主的決定の政治学――リベラリズムとポピュリズム』森脇俊雅訳、芦書房、1991
verified: https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0716712458 ; syllabus use: https://spia.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Ainsworth-Spring-25-8000.pdf ; translation: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/ウィリアム・ライカー

citation: Grofman, B., Owen, G., & Feld, S. L. (1983). Thirteen theorems in search of the truth. *Theory and Decision*, 15(3), 261–278. doi:10.1007/BF00125672
why: This paper states and extends the Condorcet jury theorem: if voters are independently more likely than not to be right, majority accuracy goes to 1 as the group grows. It then works out what happens with unequal competence, weighted votes, and correlated judgments. It is the epistemic counterpart to Arrow: aggregation as information pooling rather than preference aggregation. It is also the formal ancestor of "wisdom of crowds" and ensemble or majority-vote labeling with LLMs.

citation: Ostrom, E. (1990). *Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action*. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/CBO9780511807763
why: Ostrom answers Hardin and Olson empirically. Communities in Swiss and Japanese mountain commons, Spanish huertas, and Philippine irrigation systems sustain shared resources for centuries without privatization or a Leviathan. They do it with self-made rules that share recognizable "design principles" (monitoring, graduated sanctions, conflict resolution, recognized rights to organize). The book won her the Nobel and is the key text for collective action that works.
focus: "Reflections on the commons"; "An institutional approach to the study of self-organization and self-governance in CPR situations"; "Analyzing long-enduring, self-organized, and self-governed CPRs" (design principles); "Analyzing institutional change".
translation: 『コモンズのガバナンス――人びとの協働と制度の進化』原田禎夫・齋藤暖生・嶋田大作訳、晃洋書房、2022
verified: https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511807763 (chapter titles via Crossref ISBN 9780511807763) ; translation: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/エリノア・オストロム

citation: Kuran, T. (1991). Now out of never: The element of surprise in the East European Revolution of 1989. *World Politics*, 44(1), 7–48. doi:10.2307/2010422
why: People hide their true political preferences when expressing them is costly ("preference falsification"). Public opinion can therefore look stable while private discontent builds, until a small shift in thresholds sets off a cascade. This is why revolutions surprise even the people who make them. The paper is a canonical model of how private beliefs, public signals, and coordination interact, and it maps directly onto threshold models and pluralistic ignorance.

citation: Fearon, J. D. (1995). Rationalist explanations for war. *International Organization*, 49(3), 379–414. doi:10.1017/S0020818300033324
why: War is costly, so rational states should always prefer some negotiated settlement. Fearon shows that fighting happens anyway because of private information combined with incentives to misrepresent it, commitment problems, or indivisible issues. This is the clearest demonstration in political science that conflict is often an information and credibility problem, and it carries over to any bargaining between groups.

citation: Converse, P. E. (1964). The nature of belief systems in mass publics. In D. E. Apter (Ed.), *Ideology and Discontent* (pp. 206–261). New York: Free Press. Reprinted in *Critical Review*, 18(1–3), 1–74 (2006). doi:10.1080/08913810608443650
why: Using panel surveys, Converse finds that most citizens' political attitudes are weakly "constrained" (they do not hang together ideologically) and unstable over time, as if many respondents answered at random ("non-attitudes"). Coherent belief systems are confined to a thin, informed elite. This is the founding challenge of public-opinion research, and every later text in this strand is partly a reply to it.
focus: whole (pp. 206–261), especially the sections on constraint and on the stability of responses across panel waves.

citation: Zaller, J. R. (1992). *The Nature and Origins of Mass Opinion*. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/CBO9780511818691
why: Zaller's Receive–Accept–Sample (RAS) model treats a survey answer as a sample from whatever considerations are at the top of the head. Those considerations come from elite messages that a person has received (which depends on political awareness) and accepted (which depends on predispositions). It explains opinion instability, framing effects, and the non-monotonic "most persuadable are the moderately aware" pattern. It is the most important formal account of how elite communication becomes mass opinion.
focus: Chs. 1–5 and 7 (as assigned in MIT 17.200); Ch. 1 "Introduction: The fragmented state of opinion research".

citation: Lupia, A., & McCubbins, M. D. (1998). *The Democratic Dilemma: Can Citizens Learn What They Need to Know?* Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
why: Lupia and McCubbins argue that the real question is not how much citizens know but whether they can learn what they need from others. Using game theory and experiments, they show that a listener can be persuaded by a speaker only if the listener believes the speaker is knowledgeable and shares the listener's interests, or if external forces (penalties for lying, verification, costly effort) make the message credible. This is the theory of cues and trust, and it ties political competence to cheap talk and signaling.

citation: Bartels, L. M. (2002). Beyond the running tally: Partisan bias in political perceptions. *Political Behavior*, 24(2), 117–150. doi:10.1023/A:1021226224601
why: Bartels contrasts "running tally" (Bayesian-style) accounts of partisanship with evidence that partisans perceive objective facts (inflation, unemployment) differently. Partisanship is not just updated by information; it filters the information itself. Opinions therefore need not converge as evidence accumulates, which is a central result for misinformation and polarization research.

citation: Taber, C. S., & Lodge, M. (2006). Motivated skepticism in the evaluation of political beliefs. *American Journal of Political Science*, 50(3), 755–769. doi:10.1111/j.1540-5907.2006.00214.x
why: In experiments on affirmative action and gun control, participants rated attitude-congruent arguments as stronger, argued against incongruent ones, and sought out confirming sources. Attitudes became more extreme after balanced information, especially among the most sophisticated. This is the canonical demonstration of motivated reasoning in politics.

citation: Chong, D., & Druckman, J. N. (2007). Framing theory. *Annual Review of Political Science*, 10, 103–126. doi:10.1146/annurev.polisci.10.072805.103054
why: This is the standard review of framing effects in political science. It defines frames as shifts in the weight people give to different considerations, separates framing from persuasion and priming, and sets out the conditions under which frames work: strength, competition, repetition, and predispositions. It is the most direct bridge between political science and Kunhao's framing and crisis-communication work.

citation: Kahan, D. M. (2013). Ideology, motivated reasoning, and cognitive reflection. *Judgment and Decision Making*, 8(4), 407–424. doi:10.1017/S1930297500005271
why: Kahan tests whether ideologically motivated reasoning comes from low cognitive reflection, a "bounded rationality" deficit. He finds the opposite: people higher in cognitive reflection show more identity-protective reasoning, not less. This is the core result behind the cultural-cognition account of polarization on climate change and other science-policy issues.

citation: Achen, C. H., & Bartels, L. M. (2016). *Democracy for Realists: Why Elections Do Not Produce Responsive Government*. Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press. doi:10.1515/9781400882731
why: Achen and Bartels argue that both the "folk theory" of democracy (voters choose policies) and the retrospective-voting fallback (voters reward and punish performance) fail empirically. Voters punish incumbents for droughts and shark attacks, and their partisanship is a group identity rather than the product of policy reasoning. It is the most-assigned contemporary synthesis of public-opinion research and a direct heir of Converse.
focus: Chs. 1–2 and 5–6 (as assigned in MIT 17.200); Ch. 5 "Blind Retrospection: Electoral Responses to Droughts, Floods, and Shark Attacks".

citation: Prior, M. (2007). *Post-Broadcast Democracy: How Media Choice Increases Inequality in Political Involvement and Polarizes Elections*. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/CBO9781139878425
why: Under broadcast TV, people with little interest in politics absorbed news by accident. Cable and the internet let them switch to entertainment, which widened the knowledge and turnout gaps and left a more partisan electorate. The key variable is relative preference for news versus entertainment. This is the canonical account of how the information environment changes who becomes informed.
focus: Ch. 2 "Conditional Political Learning"; Ch. 4 "From Low Choice to High Choice…"; Ch. 7 "Partisan Polarization in the High-Choice Media Environment" (assigned in MIT 17.200 and Rochester PSC 541).

citation: Iyengar, S., Sood, G., & Lelkes, Y. (2012). Affect, not ideology: A social identity perspective on polarization. *Public Opinion Quarterly*, 76(3), 405–431. doi:10.1093/poq/nfs038
why: The paper redefines mass polarization as social distance, meaning how much partisans dislike and distrust the other side, rather than how far apart their policy views are. It documents a sharp rise in that dislike, only loosely tied to policy disagreement and linked to negative campaigning. It launched the affective-polarization literature.

citation: Iyengar, S., Lelkes, Y., Levendusky, M., Malhotra, N., & Westwood, S. J. (2019). The origins and consequences of affective polarization in the United States. *Annual Review of Political Science*, 22, 129–146. doi:10.1146/annurev-polisci-051117-073034
why: This is the standard review of affective polarization: how it is measured (feeling thermometers, social distance, implicit and behavioral measures), what drives it (partisan sorting, identity, partisan media, campaigns), and what it does outside politics (dating, hiring, trust). Read it to get the current state of the field in one sitting.

citation: Bail, C. A., Argyle, L. P., Brown, T. W., Bumpus, J. P., Chen, H., Hunzaker, M. B. F., Lee, J., Mann, M., Merhout, F., & Volfovsky, A. (2018). Exposure to opposing views on social media can increase political polarization. *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, 115(37), 9216–9221. doi:10.1073/pnas.1804840115
why: In a field experiment, paid Twitter users followed a bot that retweeted the opposing side for one month. Republicans became more conservative, and Democrats showed a non-significant liberal shift. The result directly challenges the "burst the filter bubble" remedy and is a model of computational field experimentation.

citation: Putnam, R. D., with Leonardi, R., & Nanetti, R. Y. (1993). *Making Democracy Work: Civic Traditions in Modern Italy*. Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press. doi:10.1515/9781400820740
why: Italy created identical regional governments in 1970, yet they performed very differently, north versus south. Putnam traces the difference to centuries-old "civic community": dense horizontal networks of association that build trust and norms of reciprocity ("social capital"). It is the book that made social capital, a network concept, central to explaining institutional performance.
focus: Ch. 1 "Introduction: Studying Institutional Performance"; Ch. 6 "Social Capital and Institutional Success".
translation: 『哲学する民主主義――伝統と改革の市民的構造』河田潤一訳、NTT出版、2001
verified: https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400820740 (chapter titles via Crossref) ; translation: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/ロバート・パットナム

citation: Acemoglu, D., & Robinson, J. A. (2012). *Why Nations Fail: The Origins of Power, Prosperity, and Poverty*. New York: Crown Publishers.
why: This is a popular synthesis of the institutionalist political-economy program by two of the 2024 Nobel laureates. "Inclusive" political and economic institutions sustain growth, while "extractive" ones serve narrow elites, and critical junctures plus path dependence explain divergence between countries. It is accessible context for the institutions-and-development debate, but long on narrative compared with their formal work.
translation: 『国家はなぜ衰退するのか：権力・繁栄・貧困の起源』上・下、鬼澤忍訳、早川書房、2013
verified: https://openlibrary.org/isbn/0307719219 ; translation: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/ダロン・アセモグル

citation: King, G., Keohane, R. O., & Verba, S. (1994). *Designing Social Inquiry: Scientific Inference in Qualitative Research*. Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press. doi:10.1515/9781400821211
why: "KKV" argues that qualitative and quantitative research share one logic of descriptive and causal inference. Its lessons include defining observable implications, avoiding selection on the dependent variable, and increasing the number of observations. It shaped political-science methods training for a generation, and the debates it provoked are part of the canon too.
focus: Ch. 1 "The Science in Social Science"; Ch. 2 "Descriptive Inference"; Ch. 3 "Causality and Causal Inference"; Ch. 4 "Determining What to Observe".
translation: 『社会科学のリサーチ・デザイン――定性的研究における科学的推論』真渕勝監訳、勁草書房、2004
verified: https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400821211 (chapter titles via Crossref) ; translation: https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/ロバート・コヘイン

citation: Grimmer, J., & Stewart, B. M. (2013). Text as data: The promise and pitfalls of automatic content analysis methods for political texts. *Political Analysis*, 21(3), 267–297. doi:10.1093/pan/mps028
why: This is the field-defining survey of automated text analysis in political science, covering dictionaries, supervised classification, clustering and topic models, and ideological scaling. It is built around four principles, including "all quantitative models of language are wrong—but some are useful" and "validate, validate, validate". It remains the methodological touchstone for LLM-based labeling papers.

citation: Grimmer, J., Roberts, M. E., & Stewart, B. M. (2022). *Text as Data: A New Framework for Machine Learning and the Social Sciences*. Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press.
why: The book reorganizes computational text analysis around research tasks rather than algorithms: selection and representation, discovery, measurement, and inference. It treats text as outcome, treatment, and confounder for causal inference. It is the most direct bridge between Kunhao's daily Python/NLP practice and the standards political science applies to inferences drawn from text.
focus: Part I (Chs. 1–2); Ch. 3 "Principles of Selection and Representation"; Ch. 7 "The Vector Space Model and Similarity Metrics"; Ch. 8 "Distributed Representations of Words"; Ch. 15 "Principles of Measurement"; Ch. 20 "Checking Performance"; Part V (Chs. 22–27, Inference).

citation: Ramseyer, J. M., & Rosenbluth, F. M. (1993). *Japan's Political Marketplace*. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press.
why: This is the rational-choice and principal–agent reading of postwar Japan. LDP dominance, factions, the bureaucracy, and the courts are explained as outcomes of the single non-transferable vote (SNTV) electoral system and of politicians delegating to, and controlling, bureaucrats. It is a controversial counterpoint to "bureaucratic dominance" accounts and a worked example of strand 2's tools applied to Japan.

citation: Krauss, E. S., & Pekkanen, R. J. (2011). *The Rise and Fall of Japan's LDP: Political Party Organizations as Historical Institutions*. Ithaca, NY: Cornell University Press.
why: The book explains how the LDP's distinctive organizations (kōenkai personal support groups, factions, PARC policy committees) arose under SNTV, and why they persisted or changed after the 1994 electoral reform. It combines rational-choice and historical-institutionalist reasoning, and it is the standard account of how Japanese party politics works.

citation: Dennett, D. C. (1987). *The Intentional Stance*. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press (A Bradford Book), xi + 388 pp.
why: Dennett argues that to have beliefs and desires is to be a system whose behaviour can be reliably predicted by treating it as a rational agent: you take the "intentional stance" instead of the physical or design stance. This is the philosophical root of every rational-agent model of ToM (inverse planning, the naive utility calculus) and of the question of when it pays to treat an LLM "as if" it believes things.
focus: Ch. 2 "True Believers" (first published 1981 as "True Believers: The Intentional Strategy and Why It Works"); the chapter "Three Kinds of Intentional Psychology".
translation: 『「志向姿勢」の哲学：人は人の行動を読めるのか？』 ダニエル・C・デネット著、若島正・河田学訳、白揚社、1996.

citation: Gordon, R. M. (1986). Folk psychology as simulation. *Mind & Language*, 1(2), 158–171. doi:10.1111/j.1468-0017.1986.tb00324.x
why: This is the founding statement of simulation theory. We predict others not by consulting a tacit theory of mind but by running our own decision-making "offline" on pretend inputs. It sets up the theory-theory vs simulation-theory debate that organized the field for two decades.

citation: Gopnik, A., & Wellman, H. M. (1992). Why the child's theory of mind really is a theory. *Mind & Language*, 7(1–2), 145–171. doi:10.1111/j.1468-0017.1992.tb00202.x
why: This is the strongest developmental case for the "theory-theory". Children's understanding of mind is a genuine causal-explanatory theory that they revise in response to counter-evidence, much like a scientist. It is the ancestor of the "child as Bayesian scientist" programme, and so of the computational strand below.

citation: Goldman, A. I. (2006). *Simulating Minds: The Philosophy, Psychology, and Neuroscience of Mindreading*. New York: Oxford University Press. doi:10.1093/0195138929.001.0001
why: This is the most thorough book-length defence of simulation theory. It compares simulation with the child-scientist, modularity and rationality theories and brings in neuroscience such as mirroring and empathy. It is the place to see the theory-theory vs simulation-theory debate argued at full depth.
focus: "Philosophical and Scientific Perspectives on Mentalizing" (pp. 3–22); "Conceptualizing Simulation Theory" (pp. 23–52); "The Child-Scientist Theory" (pp. 69–94); "Simulation in Low-Level Mindreading" (pp. 113–146); "High-Level Simulational Mindreading" (pp. 147–191).

citation: Hutto, D., & Ravenscroft, I. (2025). Folk psychology as a theory. In *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy* (first published 1997; substantive revision 6 Nov 2025). Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University.
why: This is the up-to-date map of the philosophy. It covers the varieties of theory-theory (modular, scientific, model), eliminativism, simulation theory, mindshaping and the narrative-practice hypothesis. The 2025 revision adds a section on AI and LLMs.
focus: §1 Theory Theory; §2 Varieties of Theory Theory; §4.2 Simulation Theory; §4.6 Mindshaping; §5.3 Artificial Intelligence and LLMs.

citation: Premack, D., & Woodruff, G. (1978). Does the chimpanzee have a theory of mind? *Behavioral and Brain Sciences*, 1(4), 515–526. doi:10.1017/S0140525X00076512
why: This paper coined the term "theory of mind". A chimpanzee, Sarah, chose photographs that completed videotaped scenes of a human struggling with problems, which suggested she attributed purposes to the actor. In the published peer commentaries, Dennett, Bennett and Harman pointed out that only a *false* belief would show mental-state attribution unambiguously, and that observation led directly to the false-belief test.
focus: Target article plus the open peer commentaries (especially Dennett's).

citation: Wimmer, H., & Perner, J. (1983). Beliefs about beliefs: Representation and constraining function of wrong beliefs in young children's understanding of deception. *Cognition*, 13(1), 103–128. doi:10.1016/0010-0277(83)90004-5
why: This paper turned the philosophers' suggestion into an experiment, the "Maxi and the chocolate" unexpected-transfer task. Most 3-year-olds fail it, and most children pass between about 4 and 6. It created the false-belief paradigm, the standard ToM test for 40 years.

citation: Baron-Cohen, S., Leslie, A. M., & Frith, U. (1985). Does the autistic child have a "theory of mind"? *Cognition*, 21(1), 37–46. doi:10.1016/0010-0277(85)90022-8
why: This paper introduced the Sally–Anne doll task. Autistic children with relatively high verbal mental age failed it, while children with Down syndrome and typically developing children passed. That suggested ToM is a specific, dissociable cognitive capacity, and the "mindblindness" hypothesis grew from it.

citation: Wellman, H. M., Cross, D., & Watson, J. (2001). Meta-analysis of theory-of-mind development: The truth about false belief. *Child Development*, 72(3), 655–684. doi:10.1111/1467-8624.00304
why: This meta-analysis pools the false-belief literature and finds a robust developmental shift around age 4 that holds across task variants and countries. It is evidence for real conceptual change rather than task artefacts, and the standard empirical anchor for the "explicit" ToM transition.
focus: whole; the results by age, task type and country are the heart of it.

citation: Onishi, K. H., & Baillargeon, R. (2005). Do 15-month-old infants understand false beliefs? *Science*, 308(5719), 255–258. doi:10.1126/science.1107621
why: In a violation-of-expectation (looking-time) study, 15-month-olds looked longer when an agent searched where the object really was rather than where she falsely believed it was. This launched the "infant false-belief" controversy: either ToM is present long before age 4, or there are two systems (see apperly-2009).

citation: Apperly, I. A., & Butterfill, S. A. (2009). Do humans have two systems to track beliefs and belief-like states? *Psychological Review*, 116(4), 953–970. doi:10.1037/a0016923
why: This paper resolves the infant-vs-4-year-old puzzle with a dual-system account. A fast, efficient but limited system tracks "belief-like states" in infants, animals and adults under load. A slow, flexible, language-dependent system represents beliefs as such. It is the main conceptual frame behind the "implicit vs explicit ToM" literature.

citation: Apperly, I. (2011). *Mindreaders: The Cognitive Basis of "Theory of Mind"*. Hove: Psychology Press.
why: This is the best single on-ramp. It goes through the evidence from children, infants and animals, neuroimaging and adults, then builds a cognitive (processing-cost) account of mindreading. It treats ToM as something adults do effortfully and imperfectly, not just as a milestone children pass.
focus: Ch. 1 Introduction; Ch. 2 Evidence from Children; Ch. 3 Evidence from Infants and Non-human Animals; Ch. 5 Evidence from Adults; Ch. 6 The Cognitive Basis of Mindreading.

citation: Tomasello, M., Carpenter, M., Call, J., Behne, T., & Moll, H. (2005). Understanding and sharing intentions: The origins of cultural cognition. *Behavioral and Brain Sciences*, 28(5), 675–691; discussion 691–735. doi:10.1017/S0140525X05000129
why: This target article argues that what is distinctively human is not just reading intentions but *sharing* them (joint attention, joint goals, collaboration). On this view, shared intentionality is the foundation of language and culture. It moves ToM from a solitary inference problem to a social, coordinative one.

citation: Call, J., & Tomasello, M. (2008). Does the chimpanzee have a theory of mind? 30 years later. *Trends in Cognitive Sciences*, 12(5), 187–192. doi:10.1016/j.tics.2008.02.010
why: This is the authoritative 30-year answer to Premack and Woodruff. Chimpanzees understand others' goals, intentions, perception and knowledge, but there is no evidence that they understand false beliefs. It teaches that ToM is a bundle of separable components, not a single yes/no capacity.

citation: Heyes, C. M., & Frith, C. D. (2014). The cultural evolution of mind reading. *Science*, 344(6190), 1243091. doi:10.1126/science.1243091
why: This review argues that explicit mindreading is culturally inherited and taught through social interaction and language, much as print reading is. Only an implicit "start-up kit" would be genetic. It bears directly on computational social science, because it makes ToM a product of cultural transmission that can vary across populations.

citation: Heider, F., & Simmel, M. (1944). An experimental study of apparent behavior. *The American Journal of Psychology*, 57(2), 243ff. doi:10.2307/1416950 (end page not confirmed)
why: Observers watching a short film of moving triangles and a circle spontaneously described them as agents with goals, emotions and personalities. It is the classic demonstration that mental-state attribution is automatic and driven by motion cues, and the ancestor of every "inverse planning from trajectories" model.

citation: Saxe, R., & Kanwisher, N. (2003). People thinking about thinking people: The role of the temporo-parietal junction in "theory of mind". *NeuroImage*, 19(4), 1835–1842. doi:10.1016/S1053-8119(03)00230-1
why: fMRI showed that the temporo-parietal junction (TPJ) responds selectively to stories about people's beliefs, not to matched "false photograph" stories about outdated physical representations. It established the false-belief vs false-photo localizer and the TPJ as the signature region of the mentalizing network.

citation: Frith, C. D., & Frith, U. (2006). The neural basis of mentalizing. *Neuron*, 50(4), 531–534. doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2006.05.001
why: This is a four-page review of the mentalizing network: medial prefrontal cortex, temporo-parietal junction and temporal poles. It separates automatic, low-level mentalizing from deliberate reasoning about others. It is the quickest way to get the neural map in your head. Their longer 2003 review in *Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B* 358:459–473 (free on PMC1693139) is the deeper companion.

citation: Baker, C. L., Saxe, R., & Tenenbaum, J. B. (2009). Action understanding as inverse planning. *Cognition*, 113(3), 329–349. doi:10.1016/j.cognition.2009.07.005
why: This paper formalizes Dennett's intentional stance as Bayesian inversion of a rational planning model (an MDP). Observers infer an agent's goal by asking which goal would make the observed path efficient. It closely fits human goal judgments for agents moving in 2-D mazes and is the founding paper of "inverse planning" (cognitive inverse reinforcement learning).
focus: whole; the model section is the payoff.

citation: Baker, C. L., Jara-Ettinger, J., Saxe, R., & Tenenbaum, J. B. (2017). Rational quantitative attribution of beliefs, desires and percepts in human mentalizing. *Nature Human Behaviour*, 1(4), 0064. doi:10.1038/s41562-017-0064
why: The Bayesian theory of mind (BToM) model jointly infers an agent's beliefs, desires and percepts with a partially observable MDP (POMDP). In the "food truck" scenario, a student searching for lunch, people's graded inferences about what he wants and what he believes are captured quantitatively. It is the reference implementation of ToM as joint Bayesian inference.

citation: Jara-Ettinger, J., Gweon, H., Schulz, L. E., & Tenenbaum, J. B. (2016). The naïve utility calculus: Computational principles underlying commonsense psychology. *Trends in Cognitive Sciences*, 20(8), 589–604. doi:10.1016/j.tics.2016.05.011
why: This paper proposes that even young children interpret action by assuming agents maximize utility = reward − cost. It unifies inferences about preferences, competence and effort under one principle. It is the bridge between developmental ToM and economic rational-choice models.

citation: Frank, M. C., & Goodman, N. D. (2012). Predicting pragmatic reasoning in language games. *Science*, 336(6084), 998. doi:10.1126/science.1218633
why: This one-page paper introduces the Rational Speech Act (RSA) model. Listeners interpret words by reasoning about a speaker who chooses informative utterances, and the speaker reasons about a literal listener. It turns Gricean pragmatics into a recursive Bayesian ToM computation that predicts reference-game data quantitatively.

citation: Goodman, N. D., & Frank, M. C. (2016). Pragmatic language interpretation as probabilistic inference. *Trends in Cognitive Sciences*, 20(11), 818–829. doi:10.1016/j.tics.2016.08.005
why: This is the review of the RSA framework four years on. It extends RSA to scalar implicature, hyperbole, vagueness and other phenomena. It is the best entry point for using RSA-style speaker/listener models in communication research.

citation: Rabinowitz, N. C., Perbet, F., Song, H. F., Zhang, C., Eslami, S. M. A., & Botvinick, M. (2018). Machine theory of mind. In *Proceedings of the 35th International Conference on Machine Learning* (PMLR, Vol. 80, pp. 4218–4227).
why: ToMnet is a neural network that meta-learns to predict other agents' behaviour from a few observations. It forms a "character" embedding and a "mental state" embedding, and passes a Sally–Anne-style false-belief test in gridworlds. It is the learned, non-symbolic alternative to Bayesian inverse planning and a precursor to the LLM debate.

citation: Kosinski, M. (2024). Evaluating large language models in theory of mind tasks. *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, 121(45), e2405460121. doi:10.1073/pnas.2405460121
why: This is the paper that started the debate (preprint arXiv:2302.02083, 2023). Successive GPT models solved more and more hand-written false-belief tasks, reaching child-like performance, which Kosinski reads as ToM-like ability emerging as a by-product of language training. Read it together with ullman-2023 for the critique.

citation: Ullman, T. (2023). Large language models fail on trivial alterations to theory-of-mind tasks. arXiv:2302.08399 [cs.AI].
why: Small, logically decisive changes to the standard vignettes, such as a transparent container or a protagonist who was told the truth, flip the model's answers. This suggests pattern-matching rather than belief tracking. It is also a methodological argument: treat "AI passes test X" with the default scepticism used for animal and infant claims.

citation: Strachan, J. W. A., Albergo, D., Borghini, G., Pansardi, O., Scaliti, E., Gupta, S., Saxena, K., Rufo, A., Panzeri, S., Manzi, G., Graziano, M. S. A., & Becchio, C. (2024). Testing theory of mind in large language models and humans. *Nature Human Behaviour*, 8(7), 1285–1295. doi:10.1038/s41562-024-01882-z
why: This is the most careful human-vs-LLM comparison: a full battery (false belief, irony, hinting, strange stories, faux pas) with large human samples and follow-up manipulations. It finds uneven, task-specific profiles, for example faux-pas failures that partly reflect hyper-conservative answering rather than missing inference. It is a model of how to run psychometrics on LLMs.

citation: Shapira, N., Levy, M., Alavi, S. H., Zhou, X., Choi, Y., Goldberg, Y., Sap, M., & Shwartz, V. (2024). Clever Hans or neural theory of mind? Stress testing social reasoning in large language models. In *Proceedings of the 18th Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)* (pp. 2257–2273). St. Julian's, Malta: ACL. doi:10.18653/v1/2024.eacl-long.138
why: This paper stress-tests LLMs across many ToM tasks and adversarial variants. It concludes that apparent successes often rest on shallow heuristics ("Clever Hans") rather than robust ToM, and argues against using standard psychological tests as-is to evaluate LLMs. It is the NLP-side counterpart to ullman-2023.
